sens: Long and straight piece of metal, worked at the forge
Robust member of a powerful creature
H4300.detail:
1. An iron bar is a forged piece of metal, long and straight, obtained by hammering iron or raw metal. It represents something solid, shaped by labor. In Job 40:13, in the description of Behemoth (a monstrous creature), its limbs are compared to iron bars to show their extreme solidity and invulnerable strength: it is a material that does not bend.
2. Figuratively, the term describes the bones and limbs of a creature of superhuman power, reminding us that God created beings endowed with a strength that man cannot equal. The iron bar symbolizes here invulnerability and the dominance of the creature.
H4300.origine: The Hebrew word מְטִיל comes from the concept of forging or hammering metal. It designates the product of the blacksmith's work: a bar that has been hammered and shaped. The family of words related to this root evokes the action of striking, forging, producing something durable and resistant. It is an image of solidity obtained through the work and transformation of raw ore.
H4300.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 40:13, where it serves to describe the extraordinary strength of Behemoth, this massive creature that God presents to Job to show him the extent of His creative power. The context is that of divine discourse: God invites Job to contemplate the most powerful creatures of His creation and compares them to indestructible metals to emphasize their invulnerability and dominance.
H4300.portee: This image reminds the reader that God masters forces and creatures far beyond what man can understand or control. For Job, who is suffering and questioning, contemplating the power of these creatures helps him to reposition his anguish in light of divine wisdom and mastery. The iron bar symbolizes the order and strength that only God can create and maintain.

sens: Precious goods kept safe, buried or hidden somewhere
Something of great value that is sought after with fervor
Wealth, possession of value buried or concealed
H4301.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a precious good — gold, silver, food — that someone hides or buries to protect or preserve it. In Jeremiah 41:8, men have provisions "hidden" in the fields: wheat, barley, oil, and honey, safe from destruction.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes what one ardently desires and seeks passionately. In Proverbs 2:4, wisdom must be pursued "like a treasure" — indicating the zeal and determination with which it should be sought.
3. The word can also mean buried or mysterious wealth, revealed by God. In Isaiah 45:3, the Lord promises King Cyrus "hidden treasures, buried riches," secret wealth that he will discover and possess.
H4301.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to hide" or "to bury." It expresses the idea of putting something away, out of sight. The word naturally designates what is hidden or buried — a good kept safe, a wealth guarded secret or protected against theft and destruction.
H4301.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetic and prophetic books. In Genesis 43:23, it is a treasure given as a gift by God. In Job 3:21, it is found in a comparison: death is desired "more than a treasure," an image of invaluable good. In Proverbs 2:4 and Isaiah 45:3, the word takes on a spiritual dimension: it represents either the wisdom that must be actively sought or the mysterious riches that God reserves for those He calls. In Jeremiah 41:8, it returns to its concrete meaning: provisions hidden in the fields.
H4301.portee: This word teaches the believer the importance of seeking wisdom and God's blessings with the same fervor one would pursue a hidden treasure. It also reminds us that God possesses secret riches — spiritual blessings, hidden promises — that He reveals to those He knows by name. It is an invitation to value God's gifts far beyond earthly possessions.

sens: The action or moment of planting something in the ground
The land where something is planted, the orchard or cultivated field
Figuratively, what is established or instituted by someone as their lasting work
H4302.detail:
1. The action or moment of planting: it is the gesture of the farmer who puts a seed or a plant in the ground for it to grow. In Micah 1:6, Samaria, destroyed, will become a "place to plant" a vine — a bare and empty place where cultivation can happen again.
2. The planted land itself: an area of land dedicated to cultivation, filled with plants that grow there. Ezekiel 17:7 and 31:4 speak of a "planted" vine and a "planted" place: it is the fertile soil where the plant is anchored and develops thanks to water.
3. Figuratively, what is established or instituted: Isaiah 60:21 calls the righteous "the shoot that I have planted," meaning the work that God has set in place and that will bear fruit for His glory. In Isaiah 61:3, the afflicted of Zion become a "planting of the Lord" — the people that God has constituted to shine with His beauty.
H4302.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means "to sink" or "to implant." It primarily designates the concrete action of putting a plant in the ground, and then the resulting space from that action. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this Hebrew word is often translated by a Greek term that also evokes the action of planting and its result. The family of words around this root includes the verb "to plant" itself and various forms of nouns designating what is planted or the place of planting.
H4302.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Micah), never in historical narratives or the Law. In the concrete passages (Ezekiel 17:7, 31:4, Micah 1:6), it designates a real terrain where plants grow and where water flows: it is a physical place. But Isaiah and Ezekiel use it mostly in a figurative sense (Isaiah 60:21; 61:3; Ezekiel 34:29): the "planting" becomes the image of what God establishes, cultivates, and makes grow — His people, the righteous, those He has sown for His glory. The nuance goes from the concrete to the prophetic: what God plants does not disappear, but bears fruit.
H4302.portee: For the believer, this word conveys a profound truth: God is a cultivator who plants, waters, and makes His people grow. We are not left to chance, but "planted" by Him in a project that transcends time and leads to glory. Just as a plant needs deep roots, water, and light to grow, we need to root ourselves in God and allow His Word to shape us. This tells us that our life has meaning in His plan, and that our spiritual growth is not a matter of chance, but of intentional planting by our Creator.

sens: Food prepared with care, appetizing and delightful
Sought-after or luxurious dish, worthy of being offered to a king or a father
Food that particularly pleases the taste
H4303.detail:
1. The word refers to food or a dish prepared with attention to be tasty and appetizing. It is food that satisfies the palate. In the story of Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 27:4), Rebecca prepares for Isaac a "dish as he likes," meaning a delicious meal that suits his taste.
2. It is also a refined, even luxurious dish that requires culinary skill. When preparing such a dish, it is because one wants to honor the one who will eat it. Jacob brings to his father "the dish and the bread that she had prepared" (Genesis 27:17): it is a gift, a mark of delicate attention.
3. Proverbs (23:3 and 23:6) warns against the desire for these enticing dishes: do not be drawn to the delicacies of a man with an envious eye. The word emphasizes here the temptation that good things can represent.
H4303.origine: The word comes from the root "טעם" (taam) which means "to taste" or "to have flavor." The prefix "מ" (mem) makes it a concrete noun: what one tastes, what has flavor. The family includes the word "טַעַם" (taam, "taste" or "flavor"). It is a word that evokes the sensory experience of taste, the pleasure one feels when eating something good.
H4303.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the story of Isaac's blessing (Genesis 27:4-31), where it occurs 6 times. Rebecca asks Jacob to prepare a delicious dish that his father liked, and then she prepares it herself. It is a key element of the ruse: the dish is what must deceive Isaac and lead him to bless Jacob instead of Esau. In the other two occurrences, the book of Proverbs (23:3 and 23:6) warns the wise against these overly appetizing dishes, which can be the bait of a trap of seduction or greed.
H4303.portee: This word shows us that it is good to take care to nourish others and prepare something they enjoy. But Proverbs also warns us: gluttony and attraction to comfort and pleasure can lead us to evil. It is a call to vigilance of the heart against the temptations represented by material goods.

sens: loose garment worn over other clothes
piece of fabric used to cover and protect
sign of dignity or social status
H4304.detail:
1. A cloak is a wide and loose garment that one puts on over their tunic or other clothing to cover and protect against cold or inclement weather. In Ruth 3:15, Boaz asks Ruth to remove her cloak so he can put six measures of barley in it: it is a sturdy fabric capable of carrying weight.
2. The cloak can also refer to a sheet or piece of fabric used to cover something or someone. Its width makes it a practical garment for wrapping objects or draping.
3. In the context of Isaiah 3:22, where the cloak is listed among the precious garments, it symbolizes wealth and social distinction: it is a garment worn by people of high status, making it valuable in the eyes of those who owned it.
H4304.origine: The Hebrew word מִטְפַּחַת (mitpachat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of spreading, unfolding, or wrapping. It is a garment that, by its nature, extends over the body to cover it widely. The biblical context shows that it is an important and visible piece of fabric, distinct from a simple tunic.
H4304.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Ruth 3:15, it refers to the cloak that Ruth wears and that Boaz asks her to hold out to receive barley — a practical gesture that shows his generosity towards her. In Isaiah 3:22, the cloak is listed among the luxury accessories and fine garments that the women of Jerusalem possessed, highlighting its character as a quality and prestigious garment.
H4304.portee: Ruth's cloak in Ruth 3:15 becomes a symbol of the support and kindness that Boaz shows towards her: this fabric filled with grain represents the divine provision for the poor and the foreigner. For the believer, this detail reminds us that God generously provides for our needs.

sens: To fall from the sky in drops of water
To send, to cause to rain
To pour down from above (figurative sense: punishment, blessing, gifts)
H4305.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply: water falls from the sky in the form of drops. It is the ordinary meteorological phenomenon. In Genesis 2:5, there was no rain on the earth at the time of creation; without it, nothing grows.

2. The verb can also mean "to make it rain" or "to send rain" — it is God who commands the rain to fall. He is the agent: "The Lord made it rain hail on the land of Egypt" (Exodus 9:23). This divine action can be a blessing (the meat in Psalms 78:27) or punishment.

3. In a figurative sense, "to rain" describes anything that falls from the sky in quantity: plagues, punishments. "He rains on the wicked burning coals, fire and sulfur" (Psalms 11:6). The image emphasizes the abundance and inevitability of what descends from above.
H4305.origine: The Hebrew verb מָטַר (matar) comes from a simple root meaning water that falls. It is primarily used in the simple form (Qal) to mean "it rains" or "it makes rain." The connection with Arabic and Akkadian verbs confirms this ancient origin common to the peoples of the Levant, all of whom depend on seasonal rains. The forms of the verb vary according to the context: either the rain falls (passive sense) or God sends it (active sense).
H4305.emploi: The verb appears about 14 times in the Hebrew Bible. It appears especially at crucial moments in Israel's history: the Flood (Genesis 7:4), the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9:23), God's gifts in the desert (Psalms 78:27), or judgments against enemies (Psalms 11:6). Job and Isaiah use it to speak of natural rain and its spiritual meanings. Amos uses it to express God's judgment: "I withheld the rain" (Amos 4:7) — the absence of rain is a punishment. The word alternates between simple meteorological description and the theological language of divine judgment.
H4305.portee: This verb reminds the reader that rain is never a purely natural phenomenon: it is God who gives and withholds. Rain thus becomes a sign of His action, power, and will. It can bless or punish. For the believer, seeing the rain fall becomes an invitation to recognize God's hand in their life and to submit to His justice.

sens: The water that falls from the sky
What God sends or withholds to bless or punish
A sign of divine power over creation
A blessing awaited for the harvest and life
The absence of rain as punishment or famine
H4306.detail:
1. Rain is the water that falls from the sky in the form of drops: it is the concrete meteorological phenomenon that everyone knows. Job 38:28 poses the poetic question: "Does rain have a father?" to show that it is God alone who is its origin.

2. Rain is a gift from God, a means by which He blesses His people: it makes crops grow and nourishes the earth. Deuteronomy 11:14 promises that if Israel obeys, God "will give your land rain at the right time," meaning at the opportune moment for the seeds.

3. Conversely, the absence of rain is a divine punishment: when the people sin, God "shuts up the heavens" (2 Chronicles 7:13), which causes famine and distress. This is how God corrects and calls for repentance.

4. Rain symbolizes the word of God and its spiritual blessings: Deuteronomy 32:2 says, "Let my teaching drop as the rain," comparing divine teaching to rain that fertilizes the soul.

5. Rain shows God's absolute sovereignty over nature: only the Lord commands the clouds and the raindrops (Job 37:6, Psalms 135:7). It reveals His power and wisdom in governing the world.
H4306.origine: The Hebrew word matar (מטר) is ancient and simply means rain. The root may evoke the sound or action of falling drop by drop. In Hebrew, the related verb yrd ("to descend") is also used for rain that descends from the sky. The word is very common in the Bible, where rain is one of the most visible forms of God's action in the history of Israel, especially in a climate where it is not guaranteed every day.
H4306.emploi: The word matar (rain) appears about 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (1 Kings, 2 Chronicles), poetic books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs), and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah). It refers both to the natural phenomenon and to the divine gift. In the texts of Deuteronomy (11:14, 28:12), rain is explicitly linked to Israel's obedience or disobedience: it falls when the people obey, it stops when they transgress divine law. In 1 Kings 17-18, Elijah announces the cessation of rain, and it does not fall for three years, demonstrating the effectiveness of the prophetic word. In Psalms and Job, rain becomes an occasion to contemplate God's wisdom and power. Proverbs 26:1 also uses it as an image ("rain in harvest," meaning out of season, which is inappropriate) to express incongruity.
H4306.portee: For the believer, rain reminds us that God never withdraws from creation: He nourishes, blesses, and governs it. It also teaches that obedience brings blessing and that rebellion leads to lack. Beyond the meteorological, rain becomes a metaphor for the word of God that waters and fertilizes the believer's soul, calling them to turn to the Lord, the source of all life and abundance.

sens: Place where prisoners are confined
Gate or fortified tower used for guarding
Figuratively: captivity or confinement of the soul
H4307G.detail:
1. Prison means literally a place where someone is held captive, where freedom is taken away. It is the place of confinement and deprivation of movement. In Nehemiah 12:39, during the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem, "the gate of the prison" is mentioned: a fortified gate near Jerusalem, named so because it was associated with guarding or detention.
2. The word can also refer to a watchtower or a fortified position where one monitors and maintains order: it is the place of surveillance and guarding, not just of imprisonment. Such a gate marked a strategic point in the city's defenses.
3. Figuratively, the Bible uses the image of prison to describe any confinement of the soul: the slavery of sin, spiritual captivity, or absence of freedom before God. The imprisoned soul is separated from God by its chains.
H4307G.origine: The Hebrew word מַטָּרָה (mattarah) comes from a root that evokes guarding, surveillance, and protection of places. It is constructed as an intensified feminine noun. In Hebrew, city gates were not just simple passages: they were fortified strategic points where surveillance took place. The name "gate of the prison" reflects this reality of the ancient Near East: gates were places of power, guarding, and detention.
H4307G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 12:39. It refers to one of the gates of Jerusalem, named "gate of the prison," at the time of the rebuilding of the walls under Nehemiah after the exile. The context shows that restored Jerusalem had several gates with significant names: Fish Gate, Sheep Gate, Hananel Tower. The gate of the prison was one of them, likely marking a place where prisoners were kept or where the city's judicial authority was exercised.
H4307G.portee: For the Christian reader, the gate of the prison reminds us that even a city rebuilt in faith must maintain order and justice. It also symbolizes, more broadly, the human need for structure and authority for communal life. The Bible, by naming the gates of Jerusalem in this way, teaches us that every detail of the holy city concerns the real life of God's people.

sens: Place where prisoners are confined
Place of guard or confinement
Target or goal aimed at (figuratively)
H4307H.detail:
1. Prison: a place of confinement where prisoners are kept. This is the most common meaning in the Bible. Jeremiah is imprisoned several times: he "remains in the court of the prison until the day of the capture of Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 38:28).
2. Guardhouse or monitored enclosure: it is a closed space intended to hold someone. The prophet Jeremiah receives the word of the Lord "while he was still confined in the court of the prison" (Jeremiah 33:1), which shows that this place can also serve to contain temporarily.
3. Target or goal aimed at figuratively: the word designates what one aims at, especially in images of misfortune or punishment. Job says that God "has shot at me like a target" (Job 16:12), comparing his suffering to a target under blows.
4. Mark or objective aimed at: the word can also evoke the point one aims at, as when one "aims at a goal" while shooting arrows (1 Samuel 20:20).
H4307H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that suggests the idea of "guarding" or "fixing one's gaze on something." The basic image is that of something fixed, immobile, towards which one directs their attention. From this come the two meanings: on one side the place where one confines (what is fixed, unchanging), on the other the target or mark (that towards which one directs their aim). The family of words shares this notion of fixity and direction.
H4307H.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Old Testament, almost always in concrete senses. The meaning of "prison" or "guardhouse" clearly dominates: it is especially found in the prophet Jeremiah, who is thrown into prison several times (Jeremiah 32, 33, 37, 38, 39). Thus, it is a word strongly marked by this historical context. The meaning of "goal" or "target" in a figurative sense appears less often, in poetic passages where it evokes an image of misfortune or punishment (Job 16:12 and Lamentations 3:12). In these metaphorical uses, the word reinforces the feeling of threat or suffering: one becomes the very target aimed at to strike.
H4307H.portee: This word reminds the believer that prison, a place of confinement and deprivation, is not a separation from God: Jeremiah receives the word of the Lord there and remains under divine protection. It also shows that our sufferings, even when they seem to pummel us like a target, do not exceed God's sovereignty. It is a call to trust in God's presence even in the midst of affliction.

sens: woman of the time of the Patriarchs, mother of Mehhetabeel and daughter of Mezahab
H4308.detail: Mathred is a woman mentioned in the genealogies of the kings of Edom during the time of the Patriarchs. She is the daughter of Mezahab and the mother of Mehhetabeel, who was herself the wife of Hadar (or Hadad), king of Edom. She is encountered twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages that list the descendants of Esau and the kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had kings (Genesis 36:39 and 1 Chronicles 1:50).
H4308.origine: The name Mathred literally means "pushing forward" or "advancing," formed from Hebrew roots expressing movement and progression. This name reflects a certain vitality or determination. Although few women are named in biblical genealogies, she has been deemed worthy of mention, likely due to her role as the mother of a queen of Edom.
H4308.emploi: Mathred appears exactly twice in the Bible, always in a genealogical context: she is cited as the mother of Mehhetabeel in the list of kings of Edom (Genesis 36:39 and its parallel 1 Chronicles 1:50). These two passages are identical and aim to establish the Edomite royal lineages, highlighting how Mathred fits into this chain of succession: she connects Mezahab (her father) to Mehhetabeel (her daughter), who became queen alongside Hadar.
H4308.portee: Although Mathred is a little-known woman, her mention shows that the Bible does not overlook the women of neighboring nations, even when recounting the history of other peoples. She reminds us that divine Providence orchestrated the events of all the peoples of the Middle East, not just Israel. It also invites us to recognize the importance of women in family and royal lineages.

sens: Family of the tribe of Benjamin to which King Saul belonged
H4309.detail: Matri is the name of a Benjaminite family mentioned during the drawing of lots that designated Saul as king of Israel (1 Samuel 10:21). It is a family lineage from the clan of Benjamin, representing one of the subdivisions of this tribe. Saul, who would become the first king of Israel, was from this family.
H4309.origine: The name Matri means "rain of Jehovah" (from the Hebrew maṭar, rain, and Yah, abbreviation of the divine name). It expresses a divine blessing symbolized by rain, a source of life and fertility in the land of Israel. This family name reflects the piety of the Benjaminite ancestors.
H4309.emploi: Matri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 10:21, during the solemn scene where Samuel draws lots to designate the first king of Israel. It is at the moment when the family of Matri is chosen that Saul, son of Kish, is then designated among his own. This mention anchors Saul in a precise tribal and family genealogy, showing that the king came from a respectable Benjaminite lineage.

sens: Direct question to identify one or more persons
Indirect question: what is unknown about a person
Expression of wish or desire ("would that" or "if only")
Rhetorical question to express impossibility or uniqueness
Indefinite relative: "whoever," "the one who"
H4310.detail:
1. The word poses the fundamental question: which person? It is used when seeking to know someone's identity. "Who told you that you were naked?" (Genesis 3:11) asks Adam to identify who informed him. It is the simplest question to designate a person.

2. Sometimes, a question is reported without seeking an immediate answer: "Who can find it?" (Proverbs 20:6) poses the question as a hidden assertion — there is doubt that it can be found. Here, the inquiry serves to express doubt or a riddle.

3. In Hebrew, the interrogative can express an intense wish: "Oh! if only I were the master" (Judges 9:29) — the word "oh" conveys this feeling. It is a poetic way of saying "would that".

4. A question can be purely rhetorical: "Who can see it?" (Job 34:29) does not seek an answer — it is a way of saying "no one can." Similarly, "Who is like you among the gods?" (Exodus 15:11) does not expect a response: it is an exclamation of uniqueness.

5. The word can also designate "the one who," "whoever": "Who among them has declared these things?" (Isaiah 48:14) seeks the man who predicted this — it is a relative without an explicit antecedent.
H4310.origine: The word הִי (mi) is a primitive interrogative pronoun in Hebrew, likely related to the root meaning "movement" or "quest." It is found in other Semitic languages. This simple little word translates a great human need: to know the identity of the other. It can also take on an optative turn (expressing a wish) when the context demands it — not by changing the word itself, but by its function in the sentence.
H4310.emploi: The word appears 342 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in narratives and dialogues. It is the main means of asking a question about identity. We see it as early as Genesis 3:11 when God questions Adam, and then constantly in narratives: Ruth asks "Who are you?" (Ruth 3:9), David questions "Who am I?" (1 Samuel 3:17). In poetry and among the prophets, it takes on a broader hue: the question becomes rhetorical, an expression of doubt or admiration. With context, the same word takes on different nuances — simple inquiry, doubt, wish, or hidden assertion.
H4310.portee: This little word reminds us that biblical texts are primarily living words — people speaking to each other, questioning each other, seeking to know one another. By rereading the dialogues of the Bible, we enter into the real lives of the characters. The questions posed by "who" also reveal great human concerns: who am I? who can I trust? who can help me? These inquiries still resonate with us today.

sens: city of Moab, on the borders of Transjordan
site of battle and military confrontation
city of plains and pastures
H4311.detail:
1. Médeba is an ancient city located in the land of Moab, in Transjordan, not far from Heshbon. It notably appears in the descriptions of the borders and territories assigned to the tribes of Israel after the conquest, particularly for Reuben (Joshua 13:9, 13:16).
2. The city is the site of significant military combats: during Israel's victory over Sihon, king of the Amorites (Numbers 21:30), and during the great battle where the Ammonites called for reinforcements to confront Israel (1 Chronicles 19:7).
3. It is also mentioned in the context of divine judgment: the prophet Isaiah refers to it in a lamentation over Moab, alongside other cities, as a place where mourning and disaster fall (Isaiah 15:2).
H4311.origine: The name means "water of rest" in Hebrew, a reference to the springs and abundant water in this region of plains. The city was a place of stability and resources, hence its association with water — a vital element in the desert. Its geographical location, about six kilometers southwest of Heshbon, made it an important strategic point.
H4311.emploi: Médeba appears five times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first mentioned during Israel's conquest over Sihon (Numbers 21:30), then in the accounts of land allocation: Joshua speaks of it twice in the context of the borders of Reuben (Joshua 13:9, 13:16). It is also the site of a great battle where Israel confronts the Ammonites and their allies (1 Chronicles 19:7). Finally, the prophet Isaiah mentions it in a vision of judgment on Moab (Isaiah 15:2), showing that the city remains significant in Israel's consciousness many centuries after the conquest.

sens: one of the seventy elders of Israel in the desert
man who prophesied without going to the tent of meeting
H4312.detail: Médad is one of the seventy elders to whom God communicated the prophetic Spirit of Moses in the desert (Numbers 11:26). Unlike the others, he did not leave the camp to go to the tent of meeting, but he still prophesied in the camp with Eldad, which surprised a young boy who ran to announce it to Moses (Numbers 11:27).
H4312.origine: The name Médad means "love" or "one who loves" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes affection and tenderness. Médad appears only in the account of Numbers 11, where he embodies the sovereign action of the Spirit of God that acts beyond expected forms and protocols.
H4312.emploi: Médad is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in Numbers 11. He is presented as one of the seventy elders to whom God granted the Spirit of Moses to help him govern the people. What distinguishes him is that he did not follow the summons to the tent of meeting, yet the Spirit of God reached him in the camp itself, showing that the divine presence is not tied to places or human protocols.
H4312.portee: The story of Médad reminds us that the Spirit of God blows where He wills and cannot be confined to our frameworks or expectations. It teaches that prophecy and divine power do not depend on our perfect obedience to details, but on the sovereign will of God. It is an invitation not to judge too quickly based on appearances, but to recognize the work of God, even when it surprises us.

sens: City of the tribe of Dan in Palestine
H4313.detail: Mé-Jarkon is a city that is part of the territory assigned to the tribe of Dan during the division of Canaan. It was located near Joppa (the future Jaffa), on the Mediterranean coast. The name literally means "waters of the yellow" in Hebrew, which likely refers to a spring or watercourse with characteristic yellowish waters in the area.
H4313.origine: The Hebrew name מֵי הַיַּרְקוֹן is composed of meï ("waters") and yarqon ("yellow, yellowish"), referring to the natural coloration of the waters of the place. This topography reveals how the Israelites named places according to their striking visible and geographical characteristics.
H4313.emploi: Mé-Jarkon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:46, in the text that lists the cities and borders belonging to the tribe of Dan. It is mentioned alongside Rakkon, both located near Joppa. It serves as a geographical landmark that shows the extent of the Danite territory towards the Mediterranean coast.

sens: Man living in the time of the Patriarchs, ancestor of the wife of the king of Edom Hadad
H4314.detail: 1. Mézahab is a man mentioned in the genealogical tree of the kings of Edom. He is the grandfather of Méhethabeel, the wife of King Hadad (Genesis 36:39 and 1 Chronicles 1:50). His name appears only once in each of these two parallel passages, as a link in a genealogical chain that traces back to the origins of the Edomite people.
H4314.origine: The name Mézahab literally means "waters of gold" in Hebrew (mé = waters, zahav = gold). It is a poetic and rare name, likely related to a region or a striking feature, such as springs or rivers from which gold was extracted. It reflects the culture of the ancient Semitic peoples of the Levant, where proper names often contained images of nature or wealth.
H4314.emploi: Mézahab is cited twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists of the kings of Edom. He appears in Genesis 36:39 and in 1 Chronicles 1:50, two parallel passages that provide the same dynastic inventory. In both cases, he is presented as the father of Matred and the grandfather of Méhethabeel, the wife of King Hadad, the last king of Edom named in these lists. His role is purely genealogical: he is never the subject of an action or judgment, but simply an ancestor whose descendants married a king.

sens: What is the best, the most excellent in a category
Land, region, or territory of superior quality
Livestock or product of superior quality
What is most esteemed, what one values the most
H4315.detail:
1. The word denotes what surpasses in quality or excellence: the best among several things of the same type. In Genesis 47:6, Pharaoh orders Joseph to settle his father and his brothers "in the best part of the land," meaning the most fertile and desirable region of Egypt, that of Goshen.
2. Applied to land or regions, it signifies the richest terroir, most conducive to agriculture or well-being. Genesis 47:11 confirms: Joseph "gave them a property in the best part of the land."
3. When it comes to livestock or harvest, the word denotes the healthiest, strongest animals or products, those of the highest value. Exodus 22:5 specifies that one who causes damage must restore "the best product of his field and vineyard."
4. The word can also express what is most valued, what is preferred: in 1 Samuel 15:9, Saul and the people "spared... the best sheep, the best oxen" rather than dedicating them to God as commanded.
H4315.origine: The underlying root expresses the idea of choice and excellence. The word הטוב (tov, "good") is a fundamental adjective in Hebrew; מֵיטָב is a superlative form that emphasizes the superlative: not just "good," but "the best." This form reinforces the idea of a clear and recognizable superiority.
H4315.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts where it is necessary to distinguish the best from the good or mediocre. In Genesis 47:6 and 47:11, it describes the best region of Egypt, a gift from Pharaoh to the Israelites. In Exodus 22:5, it is a legal obligation: the compensation must be the best, not just any value. In 1 Samuel 15:9 and 15:15, the word reveals the heart of the problem: Saul intentionally spares the best animals of the Amalekites, which constitutes disobedience to the divine order to dedicate everything as forbidden. The context shows that "best" here means "what one values, what one prefers to keep for oneself."
H4315.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what they consider truly valuable. In Saul's case, attachment to the "best" things blinds him to obedience to God: he believes he is doing well by keeping them for a sacrifice, but he transgresses the received order. For the believer, this raises the question: are we willing to offer to God what we value most, or do we hold back the best for ourselves?

sens: Levite during the Exile and Return, son of Zicri and father of Mattania
H4316G.detail: Michée is a man of the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return to Jerusalem. He is mentioned as the son of Zicri and the father of Mattania, who was a Gershonite Levite and a descendant of the musician Asaph. His descendants served in the restored Temple after the Exile (1 Chronicles 9:15).
H4316G.origine: The name Michée comes from Hebrew and means "Who is like God?" It is a theophoric name — composed of the word "Michaël" (who is like God) — borne by several biblical figures. This Michée in particular belongs to the lineage of Levi and is part of the history of the priests and musicians of the Temple.
H4316G.emploi: Michée appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:15, in the genealogical list of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the Return from the Babylonian Exile. He is identified as an important link in the genealogical chain that traces back to Asaph, the great musician and composer of the psalms of the Temple. This mention in Chronicles shows that his family participated in the restoration of the Temple worship.

sens: Levite during the time of the return from exile
man whose name means 'Who is like God?'
H4316H.detail:
1. Michée is a Levite who lived at the time of the return from exile, after the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, when he signs the covenant with Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:11).
2. His name, 'Michée', comes from Hebrew and means 'Who is like God?'. It is a question that expresses the uniqueness and incomparable power of the God of Israel — a profound confession of faith engraved in a person's name.
H4316H.origine: The name Michée comes from two Hebrew words: mi ('who') and kah ('like'), with a reference to God (El). It is a classic rhetorical question in the Bible, expressing that no one is comparable to God. Other biblical characters bear this same name with this same meaning, notably the prophet Micah from the 8th century B.C.
H4316H.emploi: Michée is a Levite who appears only once in the Holy Scriptures, in Nehemiah 10:11. He is part of the list of those who sign the solemn covenant that Nehemiah establishes with the people returned from captivity in Babylon. As a Levite, he was a member of the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple and the teaching of the Law. His signature on this official document shows his commitment to the renewal of the covenant and the restoration of religious life in Jerusalem.

sens: Levite during the time of the return from exile, father of Mattaniah
H4316I.detail: Michée is a Levite living at the time of the return from exile, after the Babylonian captivity. He is mentioned in Nehemiah 11:22 as the father of Mattaniah, a Levitical singer from the house of God descending from Asaph. His name means 'who is like God'.
H4316I.origine: The name Michée (מִיכָא in Hebrew) comes from the root 'who is' and the word 'God' (Elohim), literally meaning 'who is like God'. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing an admiring question addressed to God. It is found in the developed form Micaiah (מִיכָיָה).
H4316I.emploi: Michée appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:22, in a list of Levitical leaders of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is presented as a Levite from the lineage of Asaph, the great family of temple musicians. His son Mattaniah continues this religious function, indicating that Michée came from a family of temple musician-servants established for a long time.

sens: Son of Mephibosheth, grandson of King Saul
Descendant of the royal line of Israel during the united monarchy
H4316J.detail:
1. Mica is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Mephibosheth and grandson of King Saul. He lived during the united monarchy of Israel, that is, under the reign of David or his successors. The Bible mentions him in 2 Samuel 9:12 as a young son living in the royal household.
2. Although descending from a royal family, Mica lives under the authority of Ziba, a servant who is in charge of him and his household. This detail reminds us that the descendants of Saul no longer hold political power: David has established his own dynasty, and these former royal princes now live in dependence.
H4316J.origine: The name Mica means 'who is like God', formed from the root 'mi' (who) and 'kah' (God). It is a short form of the name Micah (מִיכָה). In Hebrew, this type of name expresses trust in God: the parent who gives this name affirms that only God is like himself, that he has no equal anywhere.
H4316J.emploi: Mica is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 9:12. He appears in the context of David's kindness towards Mephibosheth, the disabled son of Saul. After Saul's death, David sought the survivors of his house to show them loyalty. Mica appears as proof of the continuation of Saul's lineage despite the political fall of his family. His existence also shows how David kept potentially rival descendants alive, keeping them under watch but alive in his kingdom.
H4316J.portee: The appearance of Mica reminds the reader that even great royal dynasties can experience downfall, and that true power is not in birth or title, but in faithfulness to God. The name Mica, 'who is like God', also invites us to recognize the uniqueness and sovereignty of God above all earthly powers.

sens: A man from the tribe of Asher, father of Sethur, one of the twelve spies sent to explore Canaan
H4317G.detail: 1. Micaël is an Asherite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Moses sends twelve men to explore the promised land. He is identified as the father of Sethur, who represents the tribe of Asher among these explorers (Numbers 13:13). He is a minor character, but his appearance marks a crucial moment in the history of Israel.
H4317G.origine: The name Micaël means 'Who is like God?' — a question that expresses divine incomparability and supremacy. It comes from a Hebrew root composed of 'mi' (who), 'ka' (like), and 'el' (God). This theophoric name, very common in Israel, reflects the piety and worship of the one who bore it. This same name is given to several other men in the Old Testament (an Gadite, a Levite, etc.), but also to the celestial archangel in prophetic visions.
H4317G.emploi: The text of Numbers 13:13 is the only occurrence where this Micaël from Asher appears in the canonical Bible. He is involved in the account of the reconnaissance of the land of Canaan, when Moses chooses the twelve representatives of the tribes. Although this Micaël is mentioned briefly, his inclusion in this group shows that even minor characters have their place in God's plan. He should not be confused with other Micaëls mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament, who bear the same name but live at different times and in different tribes.
H4317G.portee: This character reminds us that everyone, no matter how discreet they are in biblical narratives, has a role to play in the divine purpose. Although we know nothing else about Micaël himself, his appearance shows that Israel was a people where each tribe counted and had its representatives. His name, 'Who is like God?', invites us to contemplate divine greatness, even if the character who bears it remains in the shadows of history.

sens: Man from the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H4317H.detail: Micaël is a man from the tribe of Gad, living at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, alongside his brothers Meschullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jaecan, Zia, and Eber. He is the son of Abihail. This Gadite Micaël should not be confused with other namesakes bearing the same name in the Old Testament (an Asherite, other Gadites, a Levite, etc.), nor with the archangel Micaël of biblical tradition.
H4317H.origine: The name Micaël means 'Who is like God?' in Hebrew: it is a rhetorical question affirming that no one can be compared to God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name and expresses a conviction of faith. Several characters in the Old Testament bear this name, as it was a significant name in the families of Israel.
H4317H.emploi: Micaël is mentioned only once in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles 5:13. This passage lists the heads of the families of Gad established in Bashan, enumerating seven sons of Abihail. The context is that of tribal lists that structure the history of Israel at the time of the division of the kingdom. His appearance in this record shows that he was a person of some importance in his tribe, but no particular event from his life is reported.
H4317H.portee: This Gadite Micaël reminds us that the Bible preserves the names and genealogies of many faithful whose individual stories remain anonymous. His name, meaning 'Who is like God?', summarizes the confession of faith that animated the believers of Israel: to recognize that God is incomparable and worthy of honor in every generation.

sens: A man of the tribe of Gad during the time of the divided monarchy
H4317I.detail: 1. Micaël is a member of the tribe of Gad whose genealogy is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 5:14. He is the son of Jeschischaï and the father of Gilead, and appears in the list of descendants of Gad who settled in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan.
H4317I.origine: The name Micaël means "who is like God" (from the word "mi" = who and "ka-El" = like God). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the divine name, expressing a confession of faith: only God possesses supreme power. This same name also designates the archangel Michael and several other important figures in the history of Israel, but here it simply refers to an ancestor in the genealogy of Gad.
H4317I.emploi: Micaël appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 5:14, where he is listed in the genealogy of the Gadites. This usage shows that the genealogies of the Old Testament preserve the names of many characters whose stories are not otherwise reported to us, but whose memory was important to the Israelites during the time of David and afterward.

sens: Heavenly archangel, chief of God's armies
Divine warrior who fights for Israel in times of crisis
Defender of God's people against the powers of evil
H4317J.detail:
1. Micaël is an archangel, meaning a high-ranking angel before God. His name means "Who is like God?", a question that asserts that no one equals the Lord. He appears in several books of the Bible as the chief of the heavenly armies, the one who fights to protect Israel during the most critical moments of its history.

2. The Bible describes Micaël as a divine warrior, engaged in combat against spiritual powers of evil. In these confrontations, he defends God's people and their interests. This image shows that the protection of Israel is not only a terrestrial matter but also a spiritual reality.
H4317J.origine: The name Micaël comes from Hebrew and literally means "Who is like God?" — a rhetorical question that proclaims the uniqueness and superiority of God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains a reference to God. Several men of Israel bore this name throughout biblical history, including a Levite during the divided monarchy (father of Shimeah according to 1 Chronicles 6:40).
H4317J.emploi: Micaël primarily designates the archangel presented in the New Testament and in the prophecies of Isaiah and Daniel as the chief of God's armies. He is particularly encountered in eschatological passages where he battles against Satan and his angels at the time of final judgment. The same name has also been borne by several historical figures of Israel: a Levite son of Baaseiah (1 Chronicles 6:40), an Asharite father of one of the twelve spies, Gadites, and other men from various tribes who played a role in the organization of the kingdom of David or the ancient kingdom of Judah. These different historical Micaëls remain poorly documented in Scripture, while the archangel Micaël is a major figure in biblical cosmology.
H4317J.portee: Micaël reminds the believer that God is never alone in the face of evil: He has an organized and powerful heavenly army. This archangel symbolizes the certainty that God fights for His children in an invisible but real spiritual dimension, and that the final victory belongs to the Lord. Knowing Micaël strengthens faith in divine protection during times of spiritual storm or persecution.

sens: Archangel chief who fights for the people of Israel
A man of the tribe of Issachar during the time of the divided monarchy
H4317K.detail:
1. Micaël is the most powerful archangel in the Bible, the one whom God sends to defend Israel in spiritual battles. His name means "Who is like God?" — a question that asserts that no one can compare to God, and that Micaël is His chief warrior.
2. A man named Micaël, son of Uzzi, lived during the time of the divided monarchy in the tribe of Issachar. He was one of the five sons of Jizrachja and is listed among the leaders of his tribe (1 Chronicles 7:3).
H4317K.origine: The name Micaël comes from Hebrew "Mi" (who?) and "Kaël" (God), forming a theological question: "Who is like God?". This inquiry expresses the absolute uniqueness of God and the subordination of all creatures, even the most powerful like angels, to His sovereignty.
H4317K.emploi: The Bible mentions several characters named Micaël. The most well-known is the archangel Micaël, chief of the heavenly armies against the spiritual forces of evil. Alongside this supernatural figure, there are also ordinary men bearing this name, such as the one mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar, who is noted in 1 Chronicles 7:3 as one of the five sons of the chief Jizrachja.
H4317K.portee: The name Micaël reminds the believer that God alone is infinitely greater than any power, even angelic. It is a source of comfort: God has placed a powerful chief at the head of His heavenly armies to protect His people in the spiritual battles that take place beyond what our eyes can see.

sens: A man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in genealogies
One whose name means "Who is like God"
H4317L.detail: 1. Micaël is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, living at the time when Israel was coming out of Egypt and crossing the desert. He appears in the genealogical list of the descendants of Beriah (1 Chronicles 8:16), where he is named as one of his sons, alongside Jishpa and Jocha. His name is his signature in the memory of Israel: it means "Who is like God", a rhetorical question expressing the incomparability of God.
H4317L.origine: The name Micaël comes from Hebrew "mi" (who?) and "kaël" (God). It is a poetic inquiry: "Who is equal to God?" which proclaims the uniqueness and divine supremacy. This same name has been borne by several other figures in the history of Israel: an Asharite father of one of the twelve spies, several Gadites and Levites, military officers, and tribal leaders.
H4317L.emploi: Micaël the Benjamite appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:16, in a genealogy of the families of Benjamin. These genealogical lists are records of the continuity of the people, essential for establishing tribal heritage and inheritance rights after the exile. The name Micaël has been given to several important figures in Israel, showing how cherished this name was for its profound theological meaning.

sens: Military chief of the tribe of Manasseh who rallied to David at Ziklag
H4317M.detail: 1. Micaël is a military officer mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when David was forming an army at Ziklag. He is among the chiefs of thousands of Manasseh who come to join him, making him a high-ranking figure responsible for warriors (1 Chronicles 12:20).
H4317M.origine: The name Micaël means "who is like God?" in Hebrew (mi = who, kha = like, el = God). It is a rhetorical question affirming that no one is comparable to God. This name was borne by several important biblical figures: an archangel reputed to fight for the people of Israel, but also by various leaders and ancestors of tribes.
H4317M.emploi: Micaël appears only once in the canonical Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:20, as one of the military officers of Manasseh who rallies to David during his refuge at Ziklag, before he becomes king. He is presented among the "chiefs of thousands of Manasseh", which shows his status as a high-ranking military leader.

sens: the archangel chief who stands by the people of God in conflicts
a name borne by several men in the Old Testament
H4317N.detail:
1. Michael is primarily the chief archangel, described in the Bible as the protector and defender of the children of Israel during spiritual battles. His name means "who is like God?" — a question that expresses his nature as a divine messenger.
2. This name was also borne by several men in the history of Israel. In 1 Chronicles 27:18, Michael is the father of Omri, chief of the tribe of Issachar during the reign of David. Other Michaels appear in genealogies: an Asherite father of one of the twelve explorers, several Gadites established in Bashan, Levites, Benjamites, and a son of Jehoshaphat. These namesakes show that it was a well-regarded name in Israel.
H4317N.origine: The name Michael comes from Hebrew and means "who is like God?" (mi = "who", kha = "like", el = "God"). It is a declaration of divine power formulated as a rhetorical question. This name is perfectly suited for an archangel, as it proclaims that only God is like God — no creature, no matter how powerful, can rival Him.
H4317N.emploi: Michael primarily refers to the archangel, the ultimate divine messenger. In the Bible, he is presented as the one who fights for Israel in times of spiritual and political crisis, particularly in the visions of Daniel. The name was also given to important men in the civil and religious life of Israel: tribal leaders, descendants of priests and Levites, warriors who followed David. The only mention in our provided usages shows him as the father of Omri, an official under David.
H4317N.portee: For the believer, Michael reminds us that God does not leave His people defenseless against the powers of evil. The archangel Michael symbolizes divine vigilance and the certainty that God has assigned celestial beings to watch over those who belong to Him. It is a source of confidence: even in invisible battles, the people of God are not alone.

sens: son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah during the divided monarchy
H4317O.detail: Michael is one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the list of brothers of Joram, who became king after Jehoshaphat and had his brothers assassinated (2 Chronicles 21:2).
H4317O.origine: The name Michael means "who is like God" in Hebrew, composed of "mi" (who), "ka" (like), and "el" (God). This name was borne by several characters in the Old Testament, but also by the archangel Michael in later biblical texts. The same name element appears among other members of the royal family of Judah.
H4317O.emploi: Michael is mentioned only once in 2 Chronicles 21:2, in a genealogy listing the children of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is among the brothers who, according to the account, were killed by their older brother Joram when he took power, in order to secure his undisputed rule over the kingdom.

sens: the archangel who fights for Israel
a man living during the Exile and Return
H4317P.detail:
1. Michael is primarily the great archangel, the chief of the heavenly armies, who stands by Israel in times of crisis and spiritual conflict. His name means "Who is like God?" and expresses his role as the defender of the people of God.
2. During the Exile and Return, a man bearing this name appears in genealogical lists: he is the father of Zebadiah, mentioned in Ezra 8:8 among those who returned from captivity to Jerusalem.
H4317P.origine: The name Michael comes from Hebrew and literally means "Who is like God?" This question itself is a declaration of God's uniqueness: no one is comparable to Him. The name expresses the function of the one who bears it: to defend and uphold the glory of God. Several men have received this name in the history of Israel, including ancestors of various tribes.
H4317P.emploi: Michael is primarily known as the archangel chief of God's angels, fighting against the powers of evil for the defense of Israel. However, the provided text (Ezra 8:8) also mentions a much more ordinary Michael: a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the return from exile, father of Zebadiah. This is an example of how this prestigious name has been borne by several generations of Israelites. Biblical usages thus blend the celestial figure and the human bearers of the name.
H4317P.portee: The name Michael reminds the reader that God has defenders and protectors, both in heaven and on earth. It invites one to place their trust in the one who asks: "Who is like God?" — in other words, to recognize the incomparability and supremacy of God alone in the face of all adversaries of the believing people.

sens: One of the chief leaders of the angels, the defender of Israel
A spiritual warrior who opposes the enemy powers of the people of God
H4317Q.detail:
1. Michael is presented in the book of Daniel as one of the chief angelic leaders, a powerful being in the service of God. His name means "who is like God?" — a question that proclaims that no one equals God. He is a high-ranking angel, capable of contending against spiritual powers: in Daniel 10:13, he comes to the aid of the prophet Daniel, held back by "the prince of the kingdom of Persia" (a hostile spiritual force), and he remains there to fight alongside the prophet.
2. Michael is also called "your prince" (Daniel 10:21) and "the great prince, the protector of your people" (Daniel 12:1). He thus embodies divine protection over Israel, particularly in the spiritual battles that accompany the history of nations. In times of great distress (Daniel 12:1), he rises to defend those whose names are written in the book of God — an image of the guardianship and salvation that God ensures for His people.
H4317Q.origine: The name Michael comes from Hebrew and literally means "who is like God?" This rhetorical question affirms the uniqueness and absolute superiority of God: no one resembles Him, no one can rival Him. This is why this archangel bears this name — he represents the one who, though powerful, acknowledges and defends God's sovereignty. This name expresses the very essence of spiritual warfare: it is not about rivaling God, but serving His will against all opposition.
H4317Q.emploi: Michael appears three times in the French New Testament, all in the book of Daniel, a key text of prophecy regarding future times. In Daniel 10:13, he is mentioned as coming to aid the prophet confronted with spiritual resistance from the "prince of the kingdom of Persia." In Daniel 10:21, he is confirmed as the prince of Israel. In Daniel 12:1, he is described as the one who "will arise" at the eschatological moment to defend the people of God against unprecedented distress and to save those who are inscribed in the divine book. These three passages form a coherent portrait: Michael is the celestial protector of Israel, active both in present struggles and in final events.
H4317Q.portee: For the believer, Michael reminds us that true protection comes from God and His spiritual agents, not from earthly power. His role alongside Israel encourages Christians to believe that God fights for His people, even when obstacles seem insurmountable. The name Michael — "who is like God?" — invites us to recognize that only God deserves comparison and worship, while all creatures, no matter how powerful, are His servants.

sens: A man from Ephraim during the time of the judges
A prophet from Judah in the 8th century B.C.
Several other characters in the Old Testament bearing this name
H4318G.detail:
1. Mica is primarily known as an Ephraimite living during the time of the judges (before the monarchy). He had a house where he set up objects of worship: he made an ephod and teraphim, and he hired a Levite to be his personal priest (Judges 17:5). He was a man attempting to create his own cult, which illustrates the religious disorder of that period. Later, men from the tribe of Dan came to his house (Judges 18:2) and ended up taking his priest and sacred objects (Judges 18:18, 26-27).
2. Mica is also the major prophet whose book bears his name: a native of Moresheth, he prophesied during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah, contemporary with the prophets Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah. His message centered on justice, mercy, and humility before God.
3. The name Mica also refers to other characters: a descendant of Joel the Reubenite, a son of Meribbaal and grandson of Jonathan, a Kohathite Levite son of Uzziel, a father of Abdon during the reign of Josiah, and a son of Imlah, a prophet from Samaria who predicted the defeat of King Ahab of Israel.
H4318G.origine: The name Mica means "who is like God" — it is a question that expresses the uniqueness and superiority of God. It exists in several forms: the short form Mica and the long form Micah (מִיכָֽיְהוּ) which contains the divine name. This theophoric name (which contains the name of God) was popular in Israel, expressing the idea that no one can be compared to God.
H4318G.emploi: The name Mica appears 17 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Book of Judges for the Ephraimite (17:1-18:31), where his story illustrates the religious and moral anarchy of the time of the judges. He is a rather negative character: although he seeks to honor God in his own way, he creates a private and idolatrous cult that violates God's laws. The prophet Mica of Judah (8th century) is very different: he is a major figure who preaches social justice and obedience to God. The other Micas in the biblical text are minor figures mentioned in genealogies or historical accounts.
H4318G.portee: The story of the Mica from Ephraim (Judges 17-18) warns believers against personalized religion and idolatry disguised as piety: even acts believed to be religious can be contrary to God's will if they contradict His Word. The prophet Mica, on the other hand, shows how a servant of God must denounce injustice and call for repentance, without fear of the powerful.

sens: A man from the tribe of Benjamin, grandson of Saul
Son of Jonathan, father of Pithon
H4318H.detail: Michée (sometimes called Mica) is a man of the people of Israel who lived during the time of the united monarchy. He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and was the grandson of King Saul — which would make him a prince of the blood. His father was Jonathan, the son of King Saul (in 1 Chronicles 8:34, he is called the son of Merib-Baal, another name for Jonathan). Michée had at least four sons: Pithon, Melech, Thaeréa, and Ahaz (1 Chronicles 8:35 and 9:41).
H4318H.origine: The name Michée means "Who is like God?" in Hebrew — a question that asserts that no one can be like God. This name was borne by several characters in the history of Israel, notably by the prophet of the northern and southern kingdoms. Here, it refers to a descendant of the house of Saul.
H4318H.emploi: This Michée appears four times in the Bible, always in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles (8:34-35 and 9:40-41), where the lineage of Jonathan, son of Saul, is traced. These genealogical lists show that even after the fall of the house of Saul, his descendants continued to live in Israel and multiplied. Michée represents an intermediate generation between Jonathan (the son of King Saul) and his own children.

sens: A man from the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
H4318I.detail: 1. Michée is a man from the tribe of Reuben mentioned only once in the Bible, at a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms (Israel in the north, Judah in the south). He is the son of Shimei and the father of Reaja, thus appearing in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben.
H4318I.origine: The name Michée means "who is like God" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "mi" (who) and "khah" (like God). This same name has been borne by several characters in biblical history, including the minor prophet who prophesied against Samaria and Jerusalem, and other important men in the religious and political life of Israel.
H4318I.emploi: Michée (this specific Michée) appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:5, within the genealogical list of the descendants of Reuben. Unlike other bearers of the same name who play important roles (the prophet Michée, the Levite Michée, etc.), this one is simply named in the succession of generations, with no remarkable deeds reported about him.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Levi, son of Uzziel
chief of a family of Levites at the time of temple service
H4318J.detail: 1. Michée is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi, who is a descendant of Uzziel. He lived at a time when Israel was organizing temple service and priestly families (1 Chronicles 23:20). 2. Michée is mentioned as the chief of his family among the Levites: he is the "chief" of the house of Uzziel, and his descendants include notably his son Shamir (1 Chronicles 24:24-25). He represents one of the Levitical families responsible for the cultic ministry.
H4318J.origine: The name Michée means "who is like God?" in Hebrew — a question that expresses the uniqueness and greatness of God. It is a theophoric name, common among the Hebrews, borne by several people in the Bible. For this specific Michée, the name recalls the Levitical identity of the one who bears it: a servant of the one true God.
H4318J.emploi: This Michée appears three times in the text of 1 Chronicles, in chapters 23 and 24, during the counting and organization of the Levites under King David. He is identified as the son of Uzziel, brother of Ishijah, and father of Shamir. These mentions are administrative: they place Michée in the genealogy and hierarchical structure of temple service. He is a minor character in biblical history, but he illustrates the continuity of Levitical priestly families.

sens: The prophet from Moresheth who prophesied during the reigns of the kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah
One whose name means 'who is like God'
H4318K.detail:
1. Micah is a prophet from the kingdom of Judah, originating from Moresheth (a small town in the south). He ministered approximately between 750 and 690 BC, during the reigns of the kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. He was a contemporary of other great prophets such as Isaiah, Hosea, and Amos. He is also referred to as 'the sixth of the minor prophets' because his book occupies this place in the order of the Hebrew Bible.

2. The name Micah comes from two Hebrew words meaning 'who is like God.' This name expresses a theological question: no one is comparable to the Lord. Thus, the prophet carries in his very name the heart of his message: only God is truly great and worthy of praise.
H4318K.origine: The name Micah (in Hebrew מִיכָה) comes from two words: 'mi' (who) and 'khah' (like God). It is a rhetorical question meaning 'who can be like God?' This same root appears in other biblical names such as Micaiah (H4320J in the same lexicon), which is a longer form of the same name. The name expresses the incomparability of the Lord, a central theme in Hebrew thought.
H4318K.emploi: Micah is mentioned as a prophet in two key passages of the Bible. The first is in Jeremiah 26:18, where the elders of Judah remember a famous prophecy of Micah spoken during the time of King Hezekiah: he had announced that Zion would be plowed like a field and that Jerusalem would become a heap of stones. This passage shows that Micah was known and respected several generations after his ministry. The second passage, Micah 1:1, is the heading of the prophet's own book, which specifies that he prophesied during the time of three kings: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. These references allow us to date his activity and understand the political context of his oracles: a time when Judah faced the threat of Assyrian invasion.
H4318K.portee: Micah reminds us that a true prophet of God is not popular: he disturbs, he criticizes injustices, and his message is heard in critical moments. His name, 'who is like God,' invites the believer to recognize that only the Lord deserves absolute worship and trust. Micah's prophecies, particularly regarding the judgment of Samaria and Jerusalem, show how God punishes injustice, but they also contain promises of restoration that foreshadow the work of the Messiah.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Levi living during the Exile and Return
Father of Mattaniah, temple singer
H4318L.detail: 1. Micah is a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return to Jerusalem. His name means 'Who is like God,' a question that expresses divine incomparability. In Nehemiah 11:17, he is mentioned as the father of Mattaniah, who was a Levite leader responsible for singing praises during prayer at the restored temple after the Exile.
H4318L.origine: The name Micah comes from a Hebrew question: 'mi' ('who') and 'khah' ('like'), followed by the name of God. This interrogative construction expresses the idea that no being equals God in His power and holiness. Several important figures bear this name in the Bible, including the prophet Micah who prophesied in Judah in the 8th century BC.
H4318L.emploi: This Micah is mentioned only once in the provided references, in Nehemiah 11:17, where he appears as an ancestor of Mattaniah in the genealogy of the Levites who returned from Exile. He is a man of the returning people, from a family of musicians and temple singers. Although he is not a prominent figure, his mention in this genealogical list highlights the importance of the transmission of Levitical functions and temple service through generations.
H4318L.portee: This Micah represents the anonymous faithful who, in the most difficult moments of Israel's history, participated in the restoration of divine worship. His inclusion in the genealogy of the temple servants reminds us that God remembers those who, even in obscurity, serve faithfully and pass on the faith to future generations.

sens: Figure from the time of the divided monarchy, father of Achbor
H4318M.detail: 1. Micah is a man of high rank who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. He is the father of Achbor, who served King Josiah. In 2 Chronicles 34:20, King Josiah mentions him among the dignitaries he commissions for an official mission, which shows his importance in the governance of the kingdom.
H4318M.origine: The name Micah means 'who is like God' (composed of 'mi' = who and 'kah' = like God). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several different biblical figures. The longer form of the same name is Micaiah.
H4318M.emploi: Micah is mentioned only once in the Bible in the provided references: in 2 Chronicles 34:20, during an episode of King Josiah's reign in Judah. He appears in a list of high officials and advisors that the king sends to carry out an official mission. This passage situates him in the history of the kingdom of Judah in the 7th century BC, within the administrative elite of the country.

sens: prophet of Samaria contemporary with King Ahab of Israel
one whose name means 'who is like God'
H4318N.detail:
1. Micah is a prophet from Samaria who lived during the time of King Ahab of Israel. He is the son of Imlah and became known for predicting the defeat and death of King Ahab at the battle of Ramoth in Gilead (2 Chronicles 18:14). King Ahab consulted him but feared his prophecies, for unlike the false prophets in his court, Micah only spoke the truth.
2. His Hebrew name means 'who is like God,' a question that expresses a theological truth: no one is comparable to God. It shares the same root as the name of the archangel Michael, which also means 'who is like God.' This name reveals the prophet's conviction: only God is great and trustworthy, which gives authority to his prophetic word.
H4318N.origine: The name Micah comes from the Hebrew 'mî' ('who') and 'khah' ('like'), forming a rhetorical question: 'who is like God?' This phrase affirms the uniqueness and supremacy of God. It also appears with the archangel Michael and in other famous biblical names. This question, posed right from the prophet's name, introduces his mission: to remind Israel and its king that God alone is sovereign and that His word prevails over that of false prophets.
H4318N.emploi: Micah appears in the Old Testament as a court prophet during the time of King Ahab of Israel. He is mentioned primarily in 1 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 18, where he stands before Ahab and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, to answer the question of whether they should attack Ramoth in Gilead. While four hundred false prophets predict victory, Micah alone prophesies failure and the death of Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:14). His integrity and courage make him an example of a true prophet: he speaks the truth even when it displeases the king and risks putting him in danger.
H4318N.portee: Micah embodies faithfulness to God in the face of political pressure. His example teaches that the true prophet speaks according to what God reveals, not according to what kings and the crowd want to hear. For the Christian, he reminds us of the importance of seeking truth from God rather than being deceived by many but false voices.

sens: man of high rank under the reign of King Josiah
father of Achbor, an officer of the king
H4320G.detail: 1. Micah is an important man who lived under the reign of King Josiah of Judah in the 7th century BC. He is the father of Achbor, who becomes a trusted officer of the king, responsible for important missions such as inspecting the repair work of the temple (2 Kings 22:12).
H4320G.origine: The name Micah means 'who is like God' in Hebrew. It comes from two words: 'mi' (who) and 'khah' (like), associated with 'Yah,' the divine name. This name expresses a theological question: no one is comparable to God. Several characters bear this name in the Bible.
H4320G.emploi: Micah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 22:12, as the father of Achbor. He is distinguished by his high status at the court of Josiah, suggesting that he was a man of influence and responsibility. His son Achbor receives direct missions from the king, reflecting the honor of the family.

sens: Priest in Jerusalem at the time of the restoration after the exile
H4320H.detail: 1. Michaiah is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem reconstructed after the Babylonian exile. He is among the priests who participate in this solemn feast with trumpets (Nehemiah 12:41), which shows his role in the worship of the restored temple.
H4320H.origine: The name Michaiah means "Who is like God?" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name, composed of "Mi" (who), "ka" (like), and "Yah" (the God of Israel). This same name has been borne by other biblical figures, the most famous being the prophet Micah, the sixth of the minor prophets, who lived in the 8th century BC.
H4320H.emploi: This Michaiah is a priest of the return from exile, to be distinguished from the prophet Micah. He appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:41, as one of the priests participating in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem after the reconstruction. His name suggests that he came from a family of priests engaged in the renewal of worship at the temple.

sens: Man living during the time of the Exile and the Return, father of Mattaniah
Variant of the name Mica
H4320I.detail:
1. Michaiah is a man mentioned in the genealogies of Nehemiah 12:35, where he appears as the father of Mattaniah in a lineage of priests and temple musicians. He lived at the time of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
2. This name Michaiah is another form of the name Mica (H4316I), two variants of the same Hebrew proper name used to designate distinct individuals from the same period.
H4320I.origine: The name Michaiah comes from the Hebrew מִיכָיָה (mikha-yah) and literally means "who is like God?" It is formed from two elements: mi ("who") and khah ("like"), associated with the divine name Yah. It is a theological question: it expresses the uniqueness and transcendence of God by comparing Him to any other power. The same name has been borne by several important figures in the history of Israel, including the prophet Micah, one of the twelve minor prophets.
H4320I.emploi: Michaiah (מִיכָיָה) appears in Nehemiah 12:35 as an ancestor of priest musicians who participated in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is a descendant of the priestly lineage of Asaph, one of the main families of temple singers. This character is distinct from the famous prophet Micah, even though they share the same Hebrew name.

sens: Prophet of Israel during the divided monarchy
Son of Imlah
Man who opposed King Ahab
H4321G.detail: 1. Michaiah is a Hebrew prophet who lived at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. His name means "Who is like God?", a question that expresses divine incomparability and power. 2. He is the son of Imlah, a man of whom we know nothing else from the Bible. This lineage clearly identifies him in the accounts, as King Ahab calls him "Michaiah, son of Imlah" (1 Kings 22:8). 3. Michaiah courageously opposed King Ahab of Israel: while all the other court prophets predicted the king's victory at the battle of Ramoth in Gilead, Michaiah alone prophesied his defeat and death, which earned him the king's hatred (1 Kings 22:8). Despite the pressures — a false prophet even struck him in the face (1 Kings 22:24) — Michaiah refused to change his message: "If you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken by me" (1 Kings 22:28).
H4321G.origine: The name Michaiah (in Hebrew מִיכָיְהוּ, Mikhaïahou) literally means "Who is like God?" (mi = who, kha = like, Yah = God abbreviated). It is a rhetorical question expressing the uniqueness and incomparability of God. The same name also appears in the forms "Micah" (Micah the prophet of Judah, a century later) and "Michaiah". These variants all designate men whose names proclaim theology: no one is comparable to the Lord.
H4321G.emploi: Michaiah the son of Imlah appears 17 times in Scripture, concentrated in 1 Kings 22 and 2 Chronicles 18 (which recount the same event with variations). King Ahab hated him because he prophesied "only evil" — that is, the truth, unlike the court prophets who flattered the king (1 Kings 22:8). Called before Ahab, Michaiah initially responded ironically that he prophesied victory (1 Kings 22:15), but then explained in vision the truth: Ahab would be killed in battle (1 Kings 22:25, 2 Chronicles 18:24-25). His refusal to bend to power and his faithfulness to the word of God make him a model of an authentic prophet in the Bible.
H4321G.portee: Michaiah teaches Christians the cost and power of faithfulness to God in the face of earthly pressure and power. Even hated by the king, without support from other prophets, he continued to proclaim the truth that God revealed to him. His example shows that the true servant of God does not seek to please men, but to obey His word, even when it costs. The certainty with which he asserts his message — "If you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken by me" — reveals an absolute trust in the word of God and its fulfillment.

sens: Son of Gemariah and Shaphan, a figure living at the time of the prophet Jeremiah
Man who heard Baruch read the words of the Lord before the people and reported the news to the princes
H4321H.detail: Michaiah is a man from the time of Jeremiah, son of Gemariah and grandson of Shaphan. He appears in Jeremiah 36 as a witness to the public reading of the scroll containing the words of the Lord that Baruch, the prophet's secretary, read before the people in Jerusalem. After hearing these words, Michaiah faithfully reported them to the princes of Judah (Jeremiah 36:11-13), which resulted in King Josiah being informed of the content of the prophetic message.
H4321H.origine: The name Michaiah means "Who is like God?" — a question that implicitly affirms that none is equal to God. This name was borne by several biblical figures at different times: an Ephraimite during the time of the judges, a prophet of Samaria during the reign of King Ahab, and this Michaiah contemporary with Jeremiah. The question "Who is like God?" expresses a hymn of praise and recognition of divine sovereignty.
H4321H.emploi: Michaiah appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 36 of Jeremiah. His role is that of an intermediary: he hears the words of the Lord read by Baruch and transmits them to the princes. He is a secondary but significant character, as his action of faithfully reporting the message contributed to the divine Word being known by the authorities of Judah.
