He represents a link in the transmission of the prophetic message to the people and its leaders.
H4321H.portee: Michaiah illustrates the role of those who listen to the Word of God and make it known faithfully to others. His example shows that anyone can be an instrument to convey the Lord's message, even in ordinary circumstances. It also reminds us of the importance of listening attentively and reporting faithfully what God says.

sens: An Ephraimite during the time of the judges who built a private sanctuary with idols
H4321I.detail: 1. Mica is a man who lived in the hill country of Ephraim during the time of the judges of Israel. He stole money from his mother, but after confessing, she gave part of it to a silversmith to make a carved image and a cast image that she placed in Mica's house (Judges 17:1-4). This character embodies the religious disorder of that period: everyone did "what was right in their own eyes," mixing the worship of the true God with idolatry.
H4321I.origine: The name means "who is like God?" — a theological question expressing the incomparability of God. It is another form of the name Micah (Micha), the prophet of the Northern Kingdom. The same name was borne by several important figures in the Old Testament, but the usages provided refer specifically to this Ephraimite from the book of Judges.
H4321I.emploi: Mica appears only twice in the Bible, in Judges 17:1 and 17:4, both in the account of his clandestine household sanctuary. The text presents him as an emblematic figure of the religious and moral chaos of the time of the judges, when there was no king in Israel and everyone acted according to their own desires. His story contrasts with the true prophets of God and illustrates the idolatrous deviations of the people far from the divine Word.
H4321I.portee: The story of Mica shows us how, without clear guidance from the Word of God, even acts of sincere piety (returning stolen money) can lead to idolatry and religious wandering. It invites the modern reader to examine whether their faith truly rests on biblical revelation or on personal inventions.

sens: One of the princes sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the law of the Lord in the cities of Judah
H4322G.detail: Michah is one of the leaders that King Jehoshaphat of Judah appointed during the third year of his reign for a religious teaching mission. He is among the princes Ben-Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Nethanel, sent to the cities of Judah with the mission to teach the law of the Lord (2 Chronicles 17:7). He is an officer of the kingdom charged with an important pastoral responsibility towards the people.
H4322G.origine: The name means "Who is like God?". It is formed from the Hebrew root meaning "who" (mi) and the divine name "God" (el), with the possessive suffix indicating belonging. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in Israel to express faith and trust in God.
H4322G.emploi: Michah appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:7. He is presented there as one of the five leaders of the kingdom of Judah under the reign of Jehoshaphat. This mention is part of a narrative that shows how this pious king organized a systematic religious teaching system throughout his kingdom, dispatching qualified instructors to teach the people the law of God. The brevity of this mention does not provide further details about his life or personal actions.

sens: woman of Judah during the united monarchy
wife of King Rehoboam
mother of King Abijah
H4322H.detail: Micah is a woman from the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of the united monarchy of Israel. She was the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah and married King Rehoboam, son of Solomon. She became the mother of King Abijah, who succeeded her on the throne of Judah. The text of 2 Chronicles 13:2 identifies her precisely: "His mother was Micah, the daughter of Uriel, of Gibeah." Although few details are given about her personal life, her genealogical position shows that she belonged to a family of Judah and played a role in the transmission of royal power in Judah.
H4322H.origine: The name Micah means "who is like God" — it comes from the rhetorical question "Mi" (who) and "ka" (like), combined with "Yah" (God). It is a typical theophoric name in Israel, expressing faith in the uniqueness and superiority of God. The same name or a similar form appears elsewhere in Israel for other people (notably a famous prophet), but here it specifically designates this woman from the royal lineage of Judah.
H4322H.emploi: Micah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 13:2, where she is identified as the mother of King Abijah of Judah. This genealogical passage situates her life precisely: she lived at the time of the schism of the monarchy of Israel, after the death of Solomon. Her role in the biblical text is essentially genealogical — she attests to the royal lineage of Judah — but she also illustrates how women of the royal era could come from influential families (the house of Uriel of Gibeah) and transmit power by giving birth to kings.

sens: Small watercourse
Watercourse that can be crossed on foot
H4323.detail: 1. A small watercourse, less significant than a river or a stream: in Israel, these streams mainly flow during the rainy season and can be dry in the summer. 2. A shallow watercourse that can be crossed on foot: in the account of 2 Samuel 17:20, Absalom's servants seek Ahimaaz and Jonathan who have "crossed the stream" to flee and escape pursuit, which implies an accessible ford.
H4323.origine: The Hebrew word מִיכָל (mikhal) designates a small watercourse, with an image of something that flows. Its exact etymology is debated, but the basic meaning refers to the idea of flow or outflow. In biblical Hebrew, it is a term for modest running waters, distinctly separate from the Jordan or the great rivers.
H4323.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 17:20. In this episode, King David flees from his rebellious son Absalom, and two messengers, Ahimaaz and Jonathan, must convey urgent information. To allow them to escape before being caught, a woman hides them near a stream that they then cross on foot. The context suggests a shallow but real watercourse, which plays a role in the unfolding of the narrative.
H4323.portee: This word reminds us how the concrete details of the Palestinian terrain — its small watercourses, its fords — are part of the biblical story. It invites the reader to imagine David's flight not as abstract, but as rooted in real geography, in places with water, land, and tangible danger.

sens: Daughter of King Saul and sister of Prince Jonathan
Wife of King David
One who means 'Who is like God?'
H4324G.detail:
1. Michal is the youngest daughter of King Saul, first mentioned in 1 Samuel 14:49 alongside her older sister Merab and her brothers Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. She belongs to the royal family of the united kingdom of Israel.
2. Michal becomes the wife of David, the future king of Israel. Saul gives her to him as a reward for his victory over the Philistines (1 Samuel 18:27), but the story of their marriage is marked by drama: David must first leave her to flee from Saul, and although they are still married, she is remarried to another man named Paltiel.
3. The name Michal means 'Who is like God?'. It is a theological affirmation, similar to that of the name Michael (the archangel): a proclamation of the power and uniqueness of the God of Israel.
H4324G.origine: The Hebrew name מִיכַל (Michal) comes from the root meaning 'who' and the divine name El (God). It expresses a rhetorical question: 'Who can be compared to God?' This same theological element is found in other names like Michael (the archangel whose name means 'Who is like God?') and in compound names celebrating divine power.
H4324G.emploi: Michal appears sixteen times in the Bible, primarily in the accounts of Saul's reign and David's rise (1 Samuel 14 to 25 and 2 Samuel 3 and 6). She plays a crucial role in several key moments: she warns David of Saul's murderous plans and helps him escape (1 Samuel 19:11-17), she represents the alliance between David and Saul's house when David demands her return after the king's death (2 Samuel 3:13-14), and she expresses her disdain upon seeing David dance before the Ark of the Covenant, which causes conflict in their marriage (2 Samuel 6:16-23). Through these accounts, Michal embodies both loyalty to David and the tension between Saul's old dynasty and the new Davidic order.
H4324G.portee: The story of Michal reveals how women in the biblical narrative, even of high rank, are often caught in the political and religious conflicts of their time. Her love for David (mentioned in 1 Samuel 18:20) contrasts with her later estrangement and the disdain she shows for his piety. She reminds us that faith and daily life can come into conflict, and that mutual respect in marriage remains essential, even between those united by political or dynastic love.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
Daughter of King Saul and mother of five children
H4324H.detail:
1. Merab is an Israelite woman during the time of King Saul, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. She is first mentioned in 1 Samuel 14:49, presented as the daughter of Saul and sister of Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua.
2. She married Adriel of Meholah and had five sons (Armoni, Mephibosheth, and three others). The text in 2 Samuel 21:8 refers to these five children at the time when King David intervenes in a famine by handing over Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites for them to be delivered to death, in order to atone for Saul's unfaithfulness to this people.
H4324H.origine: Her name, Merab, means 'who is great' in Hebrew, expressing an idea of greatness or magnitude. She is the eldest daughter of King Saul and holds a place of prestige in the royal house, although the Bible speaks little of her.
H4324H.emploi: Merab appears only once in the Segond, in 2 Samuel 21:8, in the account where David seeks vengeance against Saul's house after the famine sent by the Lord. She is identified there as the mother of the five sons handed over to the Gibeonites. Although 1 Samuel 14:49 mentions her and other passages speak of her (she is Jonathan's sister and, in other accounts, was initially promised to David), the Segond text retains only her role as a mother, at the heart of a dramatic event in the Davidic succession.

sens: Colorless and odorless liquid that covers the earth and constitutes the oceans, seas, rivers, and lakes
Fresh water springing from a source or well, used for drinking and washing
Tears, or bodily fluid
Danger, violence, or anything unstable and fleeting
Symbol of power and divine judgment
Element of purification and renewal
H4325G.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to water in its simplest physical reality: that which fills the seas, rivers, and lakes. In the beginning, according to Genesis 1:2, water covers the earth before God separates it from the sky (Genesis 1:6-7).

2. Fresh water, drawn from springs and wells, is vital for daily life: it is drunk, used for washing, and utilized for sacrifices (Leviticus 1:13) and ritual washings (Exodus 30:18-20). Abraham offers water to his guests (Genesis 18:4), and Rebecca at the well gives drink to Abraham's servant (Genesis 24:17).

3. The word can refer to the tears that flow from the eyes (Jeremiah 9:18), or urine—a crude but biblical term for the water of life that flows from the body.

4. Metaphorically, water evokes danger, violence, and instability: the Flood destroys by water (Genesis 6:17 and following), and enemy armies can be described as devastating waves (2 Kings 3:25).

5. Water is also an instrument of divine judgment: God performs wonders through it (Exodus 7:15-20 with the plagues of Egypt, Exodus 14:21-29 with the crossing of the Red Sea).

6. It symbolizes purification and renewal: the barren desert becomes a pool when God changes the hearts of men (Psalms 107:35).
H4325G.origine: The Hebrew word מַיִם (mayim) is one of the oldest creative words in biblical language. It simply denotes water, but in the imagination of the Old Testament, water is never neutral: it is both a source of life and a formidable force. The word appears about 550 times in the Hebrew Bible, demonstrating its fundamental importance. A probable root related to the idea of flowing and movement, water is what flows, exchanges, circulates, and revitalizes. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), מַיִם is translated as ὕδωρ (hydôr).
H4325G.emploi: The word water is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with 519 confirmed uses. It appears as early as the second verse of Genesis (Genesis 1:2), where water covers the formless earth before creation. The early chapters of Genesis show God separating the waters to make the earth habitable (Genesis 1:6-10). Water becomes crucial in daily life accounts: it quenches thirst (Genesis 21:15-19), allows for washings (Exodus 30:18), and in battles, it can be controlled or destroyed to weaken the enemy (2 Kings 3:25). The Flood (Genesis 6 to 9) is its most dramatic use: water engulfs the wicked humanity according to divine judgment. The divided Red Sea (Exodus 14) shows God as master of water. Running water, springs, and wells recur constantly in the pastoral and urban experience of the Bible.
H4325G.portee: For the believer, water in the Bible is never a mere natural element. It reminds us that God controls creation and that He judges or saves through what seems beyond our control. The threatening water (the Flood, the Red Sea) becomes the saving water when God directs it. This is why water will later play a central role in baptism: it symbolizes the judgment of sin and new life in Christ. Recognizing water as a creation of God also means acknowledging our fragility and dependence on Him.

sens: Gate of Jerusalem overlooking a water source
H4325H.detail: 1. The Water Gate is a gate in the wall of Jerusalem, located to the east of the city, near a water source. It gets its name from this proximity to water, a vital resource for the city. It is in front of this gate, in the adjacent square, that the people of Israel gathered to listen to the reading of the Law (Nehemiah 8:1) and where booths were erected during the Feast of Tabernacles (Nehemiah 8:16).
H4325H.origine: The Hebrew word "mayim" literally means "water." This gate's name designates a geographical point identified by the presence of water — a spring or a well — which made this place recognizable and important for Jerusalem's water supply. The vital nature of water in an arid context makes this name particularly significant.
H4325H.emploi: This gate appears five times in the book of Nehemiah (chapters 3, 8, and 12), all in contexts related to the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the religious life of the people returned from exile. It serves as a geographical landmark for locating the restoration work on the wall (Nehemiah 3:26 and 12:37), and as a gathering place for major community events: the solemn reading of the Law by Ezra (Nehemiah 8:1, 8:3) and the celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles (Nehemiah 8:16).
H4325H.portee: The Water Gate reminds us that the life of God's people is organized around essential resources and places of worship. It is in front of this gate that the Law is read to all the assembled people, symbolizing the importance of the place as a center for spiritual renewal and community cohesion after the exile.

sens: Chief of the sixth class of priests established by David
H4326G.detail: Mijamin is the name of a man who lived during the time of the Divided Monarchy. He is mentioned as the chief of the sixth class of priests that David organized for the service of the Temple. According to 1 Chronicles 24:9, he succeeded Malkijah in this order of service: "the fifth, to Malkijah; the sixth, to Mijamin." This role was very important, as each class of priests served in turn in the Temple.
H4326G.origine: The name Mijamin literally means "of the right hand" — "mi" meaning "of" or "from" and "yamin" meaning "right." The right hand symbolizes strength, blessing, and honor in Hebrew thought. This name thus evokes the idea of strength or divine favor. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, perhaps reflecting the beneficial character associated with its meaning.
H4326G.emploi: Mijamin appears in the Bible as the chief of the sixth class of priests established by David (1 Chronicles 24:9). Although this is his major mention, the biblical text reports that there were also other priests bearing this name at other times: one who signed the covenant with Nehemiah, another who returned with Zerubbabel after the exile, and another who took a foreign wife during the time of Ezra. However, only the first occurrence is explicitly found in the Segond 1910 translations.

sens: Priest during the time of the exile and the return of Israel
H4326H.detail: Mijamin is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Israelites return from exile in Babylon. He is among those who had married foreign women and who, at the command of the prophet Ezra, agree to repudiate these unions to remain faithful to the law of Moses (Ezra 10:25).
H4326H.origine: The name Mijamin comes from a Hebrew root meaning "the right" or "the right side": it evokes something favorable or privileged, like what comes from the right hand. Several priests bore this name at different periods in Israel's history: one was the chief of a section of the temple service during David's time, another signed the covenant with Nehemiah, and others ascended to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel.
H4326H.emploi: Mijamin appears only once in the biblical records that remain to us: in Ezra 10:25, at the time when Ezra gathers the exiles returned from Babylon and calls them to separate from their foreign wives. This very specific context of the return of the people of Israel, religious purification, and renewal of the covenant reflects the stakes of the moment.

sens: Priest during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile
H4326I.detail: Mijamin (whose name means "of the right hand") is a priest who lived during the period of the exile and return. He is mentioned twice in the book of Nehemiah: first in Nehemiah 10:7 where he appears among the leaders who signed the covenant with Nehemiah to commit to obeying the Law of Moses, and in Nehemiah 12:5 where he is listed among the priests who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple and the community.
H4326I.origine: The name Mijamin comes from the Hebrew מִיָּמִין (miyamin) composed of מִן ("of") and יָמִין ("the right" or "the south," as for the ancient Israelites the right symbolized blessing and strength). It is a theophoric name that expresses a divine blessing. This name also appears in the variant form Miniamin in Nehemiah 12:17.
H4326I.emploi: Mijamin is a historical figure from the 5th century BC, mentioned twice in Nehemiah at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile. In Nehemiah 10:7, he is among the priests and leaders of the people who have committed by seal to uphold the covenant, showing his religious authority and commitment to restoring the religious life of Israel. In Nehemiah 12:5, he is listed among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel, highlighting his role in the reconstruction of the temple and the organization of worship in Jerusalem.

sens: Category or group of living beings sharing common characteristics
Kind, type, or particular variety
Category of foods or objects of the same nature
H4327.detail:
1. The word designates a natural category of living beings that resemble each other and reproduce together. This is the most common meaning in the creation narrative: God commands the earth to produce "grass yielding seed, fruit trees bearing fruit according to their kind" (Genesis 1:11), and later "living creatures according to their kind" (Genesis 1:24). It is the natural grouping recognized by the Creator.
2. By extension, the word simply designates a particular kind or variety within a set. During the Flood, Noah must bring "all the animals according to their kind, all the livestock according to their kind, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth according to its kind" (Genesis 7:14). The idea is not merely a scientific classification, but rather: each distinct sort, each recognizable type.
3. In the dietary laws of Leviticus, the word classifies unclean animals by category: "the mole, the mouse, and the lizard, according to their kinds" (Leviticus 11:29). Here, it helps to identify and distinguish the creatures forbidden for consumption.
H4327.origine: The Hebrew word מִין (min) comes from a root that means "to share, divide, separate." Its basic meaning is therefore "that which is separated, distinct, a part." The word evokes the idea of distinction and classification: each species is separated from others by its own traits. In biblical Hebrew, this term is the natural word to describe categories of living things.
H4327.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch (the Torah). It is especially concentrated in the creation narrative (Genesis 1) where God creates and names the species, and then in the purity laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy that classify clean and unclean animals by species. Only one occurrence is found in Ezekiel 47:10, in a very different context. The word is always used in a practical and observable manner: it is about recognizing the visual and natural differences between living beings, not a scientific theory.
H4327.portee: This word reminds us that God created an ordered world where each creature has its place and identity. Recognizing species and distinctions is to honor the wisdom and order of the Creator. For a believer reading the creation narratives and the laws, this word invites us to see that our world is not chaos, but a thoughtful creation where each kind of life has its reason for being.

sens: covered structure built in front of a building, formed by columns or pillars
covered entrance or passage of a building
H4329.detail:
1. The portico is a covered construction, generally supported by columns or pillars, that stands in front of the entrance of a building. It is an open space but protected by a roof, serving as a transition between the outside and the inside. In 2 Kings 16:18, it specifically refers to the Sabbath portico of the Temple in Jerusalem, a remarkable architectural feature that King Ahaz had to modify out of fear of the king of Assyria.
2. The portico can more broadly refer to the covered entrance or passage of a building, particularly of an important or sacred edifice. It is an architectural element that protects those who cross the threshold and confers dignity to the place it precedes.
H4329.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root סוך (souk), which means "to cover" or "to protect." The word musakh literally refers to what is covered or protected — a structure that provides shelter. It is a specific architectural term from biblical Hebrew to designate these covered vestibules or galleries, distinctive features of ancient Near Eastern constructions.
H4329.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 16:18. It is in a dramatic context: King Ahaz of the kingdom of Judah, facing the Assyrian threat, modifies the architecture of the Temple in Jerusalem to please the king of Assyria. The Sabbath portico, which was an honorable and visible part of the Temple, is changed or removed. This passage shows that the portico was a significant and recognizable structure of the Temple for its modification to be worthy of mention in the royal annals.
H4329.portee: This verse illustrates how political choices and compromises in the face of foreign powers can affect sacred places and religious traditions. The modification of the Temple's portico symbolizes the alteration of religious life under the pressure of political power.

sens: Action of pressing, exerting force to extract or transform something
Physical and concrete result of this action: what comes out or occurs when one presses
Figurative image: force or tension that produces an inevitable effect
H4330.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical action of pressing, compressing with force — like when one presses milk to extract cream (Proverbs 30:33). It is the manual gesture that exerts pressure.
2. It then refers to what results from this pressure: the cream that bursts from the milk, the blood that flows from the nose when pressed (Proverbs 30:33). The word names the concrete and inevitable product or effect.
3. The Bible also uses it figuratively: anger acts like a pressure that automatically produces quarrels (Proverbs 30:33). Just as pressing milk inevitably yields cream, tension-filled anger inevitably leads to conflict — it is a natural law.
H4330.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to press" or "to compress." It evokes the manual action of squeezing, exerting concentrated force to achieve a result. It is a concrete word, drawn from the daily experience of ancient life: pressing milk, grapes, olives. This physical image served to explain immaterial realities like anger and its consequences.
H4330.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 30:33. It is a saying of the wise that enumerates three areas where pressure produces an inevitable and predictable effect: cooking (milk → cream), physiology (nose → blood), moral life (anger → quarrels). The usage is entirely figurative: the wise man is not literally talking about pressing anger, but about the hidden dynamics that govern it. The parallel structure shows that anger obeys the same natural laws as physical pressure.
H4330.portee: This passage teaches that anger is neither innocent nor neutral: it carries within it a destructive power, like the inherent pressure in milk. Understanding this helps the believer see the moral gravity of anger and the importance of mastering it. The resulting pressure — the quarrel — is not an accident, but a natural consequence. It is a call to vigilance and wisdom.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H4331.detail: Mesha is a man of the tribe of Benjamin whose name appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:9. He is the son of Shaharaim and his wife Hodesh, born in the land of Moab. He is part of a large family: his brothers are Jobab, Zibia, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, Mirmah, Abitub, and Elpaal. His name means "freedom" in Hebrew.
H4331.origine: The name Mesha comes from Hebrew and means "freedom." It appears in the genealogies of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, documented in the book of Chronicles.
H4331.emploi: Mesha is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:9, where he is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy. He is listed among the children of Shaharaim and Hodesh, with no further details given about his life or actions. His inclusion in these genealogical lists shows the importance placed by Chronicles on the genealogy of the tribes of Israel.

sens: Son of Uziel, cousin of Moses and Aaron
Levite responsible for removing the dead from the sanctuary
H4332G.detail: 1. Mishael is a Levite, son of Uziel and cousin of Moses and Aaron. He first appears in the genealogy of the sons of Levi at the time of the Exodus from Egypt (Exodus 6:22). 2. He is called by Moses along with his brother Elzaphan for a delicate task: to remove from the sanctuary the bodies of Aaron and Nadab, who were killed by the Lord's fire for presenting unauthorized fire on the altar (Leviticus 10:4). This work shows that he was an active member of the Levitical worship.
H4332G.origine: The name Mishael (in Hebrew מִישָׁאֵל) literally means "who is like God" or "who is what God is." It is composed of two elements: "mi" (who) and "El" (God). This name expresses the uniqueness and power of God, a common confession of faith in the Old Testament.
H4332G.emploi: Mishael is mentioned twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the context of Levitical worship in the desert. First, in the genealogical list of the Book of Exodus (6:22), he is identified as the son of Uziel. Then, in Leviticus (10:4), Moses personally calls him to carry out a sacred mission: to remove the bodies of those whom God struck for violating worship. These two usages show him as a trustworthy Levite, integrated into the priestly function.
H4332G.portee: This character reminds us that the worship of God requires not only piety but also concrete service and obedience to orders, even in the most difficult or ritually impure circumstances. Mishael, through his appointment and availability, illustrates the faithfulness of the descendants of Levi to their ministry function before the Lord.

sens: Man who assisted Ezra during the public reading of the Law
H4332H.detail: 1. Mishael is a man who, upon the return from Exile, stood to the left of Ezra the scribe when he read the Law to the assembled people in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4). His name appears among the seven men chosen for this important function: he represents those who supported the spiritual renewal of Israel after the Exile to Babylon.
H4332H.origine: The name Mishael means "who is what God is?" in Hebrew, composed of "mi" (who), "sha" (what), and "El" (God). It is a theophoric name — that is, bearing the name of God — common in ancient Israel, expressing a question about the divine nature or an affirmation of God's presence. Several biblical characters bear this name.
H4332H.emploi: Mishael is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. He is listed among the men who stood beside Ezra during the solemn moment when the Law was publicly read to the people after the return from Babylon. This scene marks a decisive turning point in the spiritual restoration of Judah: the renewal of the covenant with God through communal commitment to His Word. Mishael represents one of the faithful anonymous who supported this restoration.

sens: Young man from Judah deported to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar
Friend and companion of Daniel at the king's court
The one who refused to defile himself by eating the king's food
The one whom the king renamed Meshach
H4332I.detail:
1. Mishael is one of the young Judeans taken captive to Babylon after the fall of Jerusalem (Daniel 1:6). He is part of a group of captives chosen to serve at the court of King Nebuchadnezzar.
2. He is the faithful companion of Daniel and the other young men from Judah. Together, they were to receive training at the royal court, but they distinguished themselves by their commitment to their religious convictions (Daniel 1:19).
3. Mishael refused to defile himself by eating the food from the king's table, food that violated the dietary laws given by God to the Jews (Daniel 1:11). This faithfulness to the Law reveals his heart devoted to God despite the exile.
4. The chief of the eunuchs gave him the Babylonian name of Meshach (Daniel 1:7), but the Bible first refers to him by his Hebrew name, reminding us of his true origins and identity before God.
H4332I.origine: The name means "who is like God" ("Mi" = who, "sha" = like, "El" = God). It is a typical theophoric name in the Old Testament, affirming that only God has an incomparable existence and power. This name expresses the confession of faith of the parents: acknowledging that no one is like God. The same Mishael is known by his Babylonian name Meshach, which probably means "who is like Aku" (the Babylonian moon god), showing the contrast between his Hebrew identity and his status in the pagan empire.
H4332I.emploi: Mishael appears four times in the book of Daniel, always in chapter 1. He is first introduced in Daniel 1:6 among the young men chosen to serve the king. In Daniel 1:7, we learn that he was given a new Babylonian name. In Daniel 1:11, Daniel intercedes for him and his companions with the steward so that they do not eat the food forbidden by the Law. Finally, in Daniel 1:19, the king finds them superior to all the other young men. Although the text of the Segond 1910 only mentions his Hebrew name in these four verses, the Bible also refers to him as Meshach, particularly in the following chapters where he is one of the three young men thrown into the fiery furnace.
H4332I.portee: The story of Mishael teaches the Christian reader the power of remaining faithful to God even in the midst of a hostile and seductive culture. Like Daniel and his other companions, Mishael shows that one can serve a pagan king while maintaining a clear conscience toward the God of Israel. His decision not to defile himself with royal food illustrates that no earthly advantage is worth the price of obedience to God.

sens: Young man deported to Babylon with Daniel
One of the three friends refusing to defile themselves with the king's food
Companion of Daniel in the service of King Nebuchadnezzar
One of the three young men thrown into the fiery furnace
H4333.detail:
1. Mishael is a young Jew deported to Babylon during the Exile, at the time of King Nebuchadnezzar. He is first introduced in Daniel 2:17 under his Hebrew name, then renamed Meshach by the Babylonians (Daniel 1:7), who imposed new names on the captives to assimilate them.

2. He, along with his companions Daniel, Hananiah, and Azariah, refuses to defile themselves by eating the royal food, which violated the dietary laws given by God to Israel. This obedience to conscience shows his attachment to his faith despite captivity.

3. Mishael is one of the three who, with his friends, throw themselves into the fiery furnace to refuse to bow down before the golden idol. The angel of the Lord miraculously saves them from the fire, testifying to God's faithfulness to those who seek Him.
H4333.origine: The name Mishael means "who is like God" or "who is what God is." It expresses a deep conviction: only God is incomparable. The Aramaic name represents the same reality as the Hebrew, borne by a young man who will live this faith during the Babylonian Exile.
H4333.emploi: Mishael appears mainly in the book of Daniel, first named by his Hebrew name in Daniel 2:17, then more often by his Babylonian nickname Meshach (Daniel 1:7; 3:12-30). He is presented as Daniel's faithful friend: together, they refuse to compromise with the idolatrous practices of the kingdom. His story illustrates how to remain faithful to God in the heart of a foreign and hostile culture.
H4333.portee: Mishael shows that faithfulness to God is not solitary: it is lived with other believers who share the same convictions. His friendship with Daniel and his courageous refusals of idolatry remind the reader that true strength comes from obedience to God, even when it costs dearly. His rescue from the furnace is a promise: God does not abandon those who seek Him.

sens: Flat and even stretch of land
Flat territory suitable for agriculture and pastoralism
Figurative sense: righteousness, equity, justice
H4334.detail:
1. A plain is a wide expanse of flat land, without significant relief. It contrasts with mountains and hills. The Bible describes the flat territories of Canaan: "They had for territory, from Aroer on the banks of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the midst of the valley, all the plain near Medeba" (Joshua 13:16).
2. These plains, rich and habitable, hosted cities, crops, and flocks. Hezekiah "built towers in the wilderness, and he dug many cisterns, because he had many flocks in the valleys and in the plain" (2 Chronicles 26:10).
3. In a figurative sense, the word denotes moral uprightness, equity, rectitude in judgment and conduct. Psalm 45:7 sings: "The scepter of your reign is a scepter of equity" — it is God's just governance. Isaiah announces of the Messiah: "He will judge the poor with equity, and he will pronounce with righteousness on the needy of the earth" (Isaiah 11:4).
H4334.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be flattened, equal." The basic image is that of a flat surface, from which the sense of uprightness and righteousness naturally derives — what is "right" morally, just as the plain is "straight" geographically. This transition of meaning, from the physical to the moral, is common in Hebrew: the righteous is one who "walks straight" on a level path.
H4334.emploi: The word appears 23 times, primarily in two distinct usages. First, as a concrete geographical name: it designates the flat lands of Transjordan, notably the plain of Moab and the plateaus of Gilead and Bashan (Deuteronomy 3:10, Joshua 13:9-21, etc.). These regions were well known as areas of settlement and cultivation. Secondly, in the Psalms and the Prophets, the word is used in a moral and spiritual sense: God's righteousness in His judgment (Psalm 45:7, Isaiah 11:4), and the desire of the righteous to walk in uprightness (Psalm 27:11). This semantic duality enriches biblical language: the plain becomes an image of the clear and just path that one must follow.
H4334.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that God judges with absolute equity and righteousness: there is no injustice in Him. At the same time, it invites moral transparency — to seek righteousness in one's actions, just as one walks on a level ground without deviation. It is an invitation to honesty and justice in all relationships.

sens: Hebrew young man deported to Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar
Babylonian name given to Mishael, his original Hebrew name
H4335.detail:
1. Méschac is the Babylonian name imposed on a young Hebrew of noble lineage, Mishael, after his capture and deportation to Babylon during the exile of the kingdom of Judah in the 6th century B.C. The chief of the king's eunuchs, Nebuchadnezzar, renames him in order to integrate him into the king's court and sever his ties to his origins.
2. This new name is distinct from his original identity: Mishael, "who is like God," becomes Méschac, which means "guest of the king" or "close to the king." This name change symbolizes Babylonian dominance and the attempt at cultural assimilation.
H4335.origine: The name Méschac is a Babylonian name, different from the original Hebrew name Mishael. Mishael means "who is like God" (mî, "who," and El, "God"). The renaming reflects the Babylonian practice of assimilating high-ranking captives. Méschac likely comes from a Babylonian formula of status or proximity to royalty.
H4335.emploi: Méschac primarily appears in the book of Daniel to designate one of the three young Hebrews who become faithful companions of the prophet Daniel. Along with Shadrach and Abednego, he refuses to eat the king's food (Daniel 1:8) in order to obey the dietary laws of the Torah. The three friends are then thrown into the fiery furnace for refusing to bow down to the golden statue that Nebuchadnezzar had erected, but they are miraculously saved by an angel. The account portrays them as models of faithfulness to God despite the pressures of pagan power.
H4335.portee: The story of Méschac and his companions encourages believers to remain faithful to God even under oppression and persecution. It shows that the name and status changes imposed by the world cannot alter the deep identity of those who belong to God. It is a call not to yield to compromises that would contradict biblical principles, even in the face of death threats.

sens: One of the three young Jews deported to Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar
The Aramaic name given by the chief of the king's eunuchs to the one whose Hebrew name was Mishael
A man who refused to defile himself by eating at the king's table
A faithful one who refused to bow down before the king's golden statue
A young man thrown into the fiery furnace for his refusal of idolatry
A miraculous survivor saved by the angel of the Lord in the flames
H4336.detail: 1. Abed-Nego is one of Daniel's three Jewish companions during the exile in Babylon. Along with Shadrach and Méschac, he embodies faithfulness to God in the heart of a pagan empire. 2. His Aramaic name, which means "servant of the god Nego," was imposed by the Babylonian king to detach him from his Hebrew identity and the faith of Israel. 3. Contrary to royal orders, he refuses to defile himself by eating the king's food, as it violated the Law of Moses regarding clean and unclean (Daniel 1). 4. When Nebuchadnezzar erects a golden statue and orders all peoples to bow down to it, Abed-Nego, Shadrach, and Méschac refuse, preferring to obey God rather than the monarch (Daniel 3:12-14). 5. Furious, the king has them thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual (Daniel 3:19). 6. Miraculously, they are saved by the angel of the Lord and emerge without a single burn, prompting Nebuchadnezzar to acknowledge the power of the God of Israel (Daniel 3:26-28).
H4336.origine: The original Hebrew name is Mishael (מִישָׁאֵל), which means "Who is like God?" The Babylonians transformed it into Abed-Nego (עֲבֵד-נְגוֹ in Aramaic), a name composed of "Abed" (servant) and "Nego" (a Babylonian god). This name change was common during deportations: it aimed to transform the religious and cultural identity of young prisoners by integrating them into the royal court.
H4336.emploi: Abed-Nego appears thirteen times in the book of Daniel, only in chapter 3 and once in chapter 2, always mentioned alongside Shadrach and Méschac. In the Greek version (Septuagint), he is called "Abed-Nego," while the French Segond translates it this way. The account first shows him faithful in the detail of his food (Daniel 1), then courageous in the face of the challenge of idolatry (Daniel 3). His interventions become more visible when the king demands a justification: "We do not need to answer you in this matter" (Daniel 3:16) shows a serene trust in God. The climax of his story is the miracle of the furnace, where he walks unharmed in the flames (Daniel 3:22-23), proof of divine presence and the courage of one who remains faithful.
H4336.portee: The story of Abed-Nego teaches the Christian reader the cost of faithfulness to God in a hostile and secular context. Despite the pressure of political power, the threat of death, and cultural assimilation, he chooses to obey God's commandments rather than human decrees. His example shows that trust in God is not naive: it produces visible results and even invites unbelievers to recognize the power of the Lord. For today's believer, he represents the courage to remain distinctive in faith, without compromising on essential convictions.

sens: Son of Caleb and grandson of Hezron, from the tribe of Judah
H4337.detail: Méscha is a character from the Old Testament, son of Caleb and Azubah, and grandson of Hezron. He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is the firstborn of Caleb and had several brothers: Jerachmeel, Hur, Jesher, Shobab, Ardon, Haran, Moza, Gazez, Jahdai, Sheber, Tirhanah, Shaaph, Sheva, and Achsah (1 Chronicles 2:42). Méscha himself had two sons: Ziph and Hebron, the latter also mentioned as the father of several cities in Israel.
H4337.origine: The name Méscha means "deliverance" in Hebrew. It carries a prophetic name that refers to the idea of salvation and liberation, important themes in the history of God's people.
H4337.emploi: Méscha appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:42, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as Caleb's firstborn and the father of two important sons for the genealogy of the tribes: Ziph and Hebron. This genealogical mention situates him in the continuity of the promised lineage and the distribution of territories in Canaan.

sens: King of Moab during the time of Ahab and Joram
H4338.detail: Méscha is the king of the kingdom of Moab during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 3:4, where we learn that he was a powerful king who owned vast flocks and paid a heavy tribute to the king of Israel: one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams with their wool. This mention reveals the political and economic dominance of Israel over Moab at that time and shows that Méscha was wealthy enough to pay this considerable tribute.
H4338.origine: The name Méscha means "deliverance" in Hebrew, an image of one who saves or is saved. Although the name carries this positive meaning, there is no indication in the biblical account that deliverance characterized his reign—it was simply his personal name.
H4338.emploi: Méscha appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Kings 3:4. He is presented as king of Moab during the reign of Ahab and Joram in Israel. What makes him notable is not his military or political acts recounted in detail, but the enormous tribute he paid to Israel, a testimony to Israeli power at that time. His name also appears in ancient archaeological inscriptions, confirming his historical existence.

sens: Quality of what is straight, even, without roughness
Moral rectitude, honesty of heart and conduct
Justice and fairness in judgments and decisions
Figurative path or road that goes straight ahead, without detour
Ease of movement or flow
H4339.detail:
1. Uprightness first denotes what is physically straight, even, smooth — without curve or roughness. This is the primary image: a flat surface, a trajectory without detours. In Proverbs 23:31, the wine that "flows easily" in the cup evokes this natural fluidity.
2. Applied to the heart and moral life, uprightness means integrity: a will directed towards good, without ulterior motives. David in 1 Chronicles 29:17 says he offered "in the uprightness of my heart" — that is, with total sincerity, without calculation.
3. Among judges and leaders, uprightness is to render justice fairly, without favoring the rich or influential. In Psalms 58:2, the psalmist asks the magistrates: "Do you judge with uprightness?" — in other words, do you truly weigh actions according to justice?
4. Spiritually, the path of uprightness is that of the righteous: direct, without detours towards evil. Isaiah 26:7 states that "the path of the righteous is uprightness"; it is the image of a life that moves straight towards God.
5. The expression "with ease" in Proverbs 23:31 shows that uprightness can also describe an action that flows, unfolds without obstacle — natural fluidity.
H4339.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be straight, to equalize." It belongs to the family of words designating what is straight, without curvature. The same root appears in contexts of leveling, smoothing. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often conveys the idea of moral and judicial uprightness — a virtue characterizing one who does not deviate from good.
H4339.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, primarily in classical Hebrew. It is very present in Proverbs and Psalms, where it describes the quality of the righteous heart and fair judgment. In 1 Chronicles 29:17, David uses it to speak of the integrity of the heart in worship. In Psalms (58:2, 99:4, 96:10), it characterizes God's justice and that which magistrates must render. Proverbs links it to wisdom and understanding of good (2:9, 8:6) — one who embraces uprightness understands the paths of the righteous. The word can also simply describe the natural course of something, like wine that flows (Proverbs 23:31). Isaiah uses it as the image of the righteous path before God.
H4339.portee: Uprightness calls the Christian to two things: first, to honesty of heart in their relationship with God — to offer sincerely, without calculation or hypocrisy. Secondly, it exhorts them to seek fairness in their dealings with others and in their judgments: not to favor the powerful, but to weigh each situation justly. It is a virtue that brings one back to rectitude, the straight path that leads to God.

sens: Rope or string used for tying or holding
Tent or pavilion cord
Bowstring
H4340.detail:
1. Cord refers to a rope or string that is manufactured, braided, or knotted, used to tie, bind, or hold objects together. This is the most basic meaning of the word, observable in all uses of the tabernacle: cords are used for tying.
2. In the context of the tabernacle and its appendages, cords specifically refer to the ropes that secure the fabrics and tents, and that hold the stakes anchored to the ground. In Exodus 35:18, it lists "the stakes of the tabernacle, the stakes of the courtyard, and their cords," showing that each tent and structure needs cords to remain upright and stable.
3. By extension or family of words, the term can evoke the bowstring, which stretches and propels the arrow — a cord under tension, carrying force. Psalms 21:13 and Jeremiah 10:20 explore this figurative image.
H4340.origine: The Hebrew word מֵיתָר (me'tar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of stretching or tightening. The word is related to other terms meaning "cord" or "tie." In the Greek Old Testament, this word was translated by Greek words meaning "rope" or "bowstring." The fundamental image is that of something stretched or braided to bind and hold.
H4340.emploi: The word מֵיתָר appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible. The majority of uses (6 references) concern the tabernacle and its accessories: the cords that attach the fabrics of the courtyard, hold the stakes, and keep the columns in place (Exodus 35:18, 39:40; Numbers 3:26, 3:37, 4:26, 4:32). These passages show that cords are practical and essential elements of the portable structure of the sanctuary. The other three uses (Psalms 21:13, Isaiah 54:2, Jeremiah 10:20) use the word in a more figurative or poetic manner, notably to evoke bowstrings or, by extension, the ties that hold a community or household together.
H4340.portee: For the reader, the cord reminds us that even the most sacred structures — the tabernacle where God dwells — rest on simple, ordinary, and material elements. This illustrates God's care for the practical details of His worship and the necessity of order in the life of the people. The cord also evokes strength and cohesion: a fabric without cord collapses, just as a community without ties. It is a humble image of maintenance and stability.

sens: Physical suffering of the body, injury
Moral pain, sorrow of the soul
Inner torment that afflicts man
State of misfortune and distress
H4341.detail:
1. Physical pain: it is primarily the suffering of the body, as when a sick person suffers on their bed (Job 33:19: "By pain, man is also chastened on his bed, when a constant struggle comes to agitate his bones"). It denotes an intense and painful sensation.
2. Moral pain: it is the sadness, the sorrow that weighs on the heart and mind. One who knows God can say "my pain is always before me" (Psalms 38:18), like a constant weight.
3. Inner torment: the pain that results from sin, guilt, or adversity. Ecclesiastes 1:18 states: "with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and he who increases knowledge increases pain" — pain arises from the awareness of misfortune.
4. Collective misfortune: the suffering of an oppressed people, like that of Israel in Egypt, of which God says, "I have seen the suffering of my people" (Exodus 3:7). It is also the pain of the Suffering Servant in Isaiah 53:3: "A man of pain and acquainted with suffering."
H4341.origine: The Hebrew word מַכְאוֹב comes from a root that expresses the idea of being crushed, overwhelmed. It is related to the idea of pressure or injury — something that crushes or hurts. In Hebrew, this word belongs to the family of terms that describe not only physical injury but also inner affliction. That is why it can mean both the wound of the body and the wound of the heart.
H4341.emploi: This word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms, the wisdom books (Job, Ecclesiastes), and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations). It designates sometimes the physical suffering of the afflicted righteous (Job 33:19), sometimes the moral pain resulting from sin (Ecclesiastes 1:18; Jeremiah 30:15), and sometimes God's compassion towards His suffering people (Exodus 3:7). In Isaiah 53:3-4, it characterizes the Servant of the Lord, who bears the pains of the people. The word also appears in Lamentations, where Jerusalem expresses its distress (Lamentations 1:12: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?" ). Pain, in biblical usage, is never dissociated from an issue: it is either divine correction, compassion, or solidarity with the suffering.
H4341.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that pain — physical or moral — is real and present in this world. The Bible does not pretend to ignore it: it names it and speaks of it. It also teaches that God does not remain indifferent to the suffering of His people (Exodus 3:7) and that, in Jesus Christ, the Suffering Servant, God Himself has identified with our pains. It is an invitation to trust and to pray in the very heart of sorrow.

sens: a blow struck on the body, the mark it leaves
injury, lesion
lasting physical suffering, disease
military defeat, setback in battle
disaster or plague sent by God
divine punishment or judgment
H4347.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the blow itself, the violent act that strikes: it is the blow received and the mark it leaves on the body. In Leviticus 26:21, God says, "I will strike you seven times": the word evokes the action of striking and its immediate effects.

2. It then signifies the open wound, the sore that remains after the blow or after an injury, with its potential for lasting pain. Isaiah 1:6 lists the wounds of a sick body: "They are only bruises, welts, and open sores that have not been cleansed or bandaged."

3. The word extends to chronic physical suffering, to the disease that gnaws: Jeremiah 30:12 speaks of an incurable wound that refuses to heal.

4. On the military level, the word means defeat, the blow dealt to the enemy in battle. In 1 Samuel 14:30, the "defeat of the Philistines" is a great victory won: the enemy has been struck militarily.

5. It also designates the plague or disaster, particularly the calamities that God sends: Deuteronomy 28:59-61 lists the plagues, diseases, and evils that the Lord may inflict as punishment.

6. Finally, it expresses divine judgment, God's punishment on a people or an individual: Jeremiah 14:17 speaks of a great wound striking the daughter of the people as a consequence of judgment.
H4347.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning to strike, to hit. The initial image is that of a received blow, of a violent shock. From the same root comes the verb "to strike" (nakah), which becomes a noun: the wound, thus literally meaning "that which has been struck." The root expresses the action of delivering a blow (military, physical, or judicial) and its results: the mark, the injury, the disaster.
H4347.emploi: The word appears 46 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, the prophets, and the psalms. It designates both ordinary physical wounds (blows, injuries, diseases) and military defeats and divine plagues. Historical books often place it in battle narratives: Joshua, Judges, and Samuel use it for victories won over enemies. The prophets Jeremiah and Isaiah use it to speak of physical wounds, incurable diseases, and God's judgments on Israel. Deuteronomy lists the plagues as punishments for the broken covenant. The meaning easily shifts from physical blow to collective disaster, from visible injury to God's hidden judgment.
H4347.portee: This word reminds us that life under sin bears real, visible, or hidden wounds. The wound becomes in the Bible the very image of judgment and the suffering of sin. But it is also a call to repentance: God strikes to warn and call back. Finally, the wounds of Christ (Isaiah 53) will be healing for all who believe. Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible articulates suffering, judgment, and redemption.

sens: Mark left by fire on the skin
Skin lesion resembling a burn but caused by leprosy
H4348.detail:
1. The word designates the visible mark that fire leaves on the skin after burning it: a wound characterized by its redness and depth. This is what the priest examines in a man who has been burned (Leviticus 13:24).
2. In the diagnosis of leprosy, a burn may show signs of this disease: if the hair turns white in the spot and if it appears deeper than the skin, it is leprosy that has broken out in the burn, and the man is declared unclean (Leviticus 13:25). Conversely, if the spot remains pale and does not spread, it is simply the scar of a burn that is healing, and the man remains clean (Leviticus 13:28).
H4348.origine: The Hebrew word מִכְוָה (mikh.vah) comes from the root כוה, which literally means "to burn" or "to be burned." It is a nominal form that designates the result of the action of burning: the mark or scar left by fire. The same root appears in other words describing wounds or effects of fire in the Bible.
H4348.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Bible, all occurrences found in the same passage: Leviticus 13:24-28, where the laws regarding skin diseases are enumerated. In this context, the burn serves as a point of comparison and medical diagnosis: it is a skin condition that the priest must examine to determine whether it is a simple burn healing or if leprosy has developed in it. The word thus describes an observable and recognizable physical condition, serving as a practical case in the Levitical purity code.
H4348.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage reminds us that the law of Moses paid great attention to the distinction between natural disease and ritually impure disease. It also shows that God does not ignore the physical suffering of the people and establishes just and coherent rules to protect the community. This law also invites mercy: an ordinary burn that heals naturally does not render a man unclean.

sens: A fixed, determined place where one dwells or establishes something
The base, the foundation on which a construction or reality rests
A seat, a residence, or a throne from which authority is exercised
A place consecrated to the divine presence
The ground or stable surface of a land
H4349.detail:
1. The word first designates a fixed, established place where someone or something dwells in a stable and lasting manner. Moses says to God: "You will establish them on the mountain of your inheritance, in the place you have prepared for your dwelling" (Exodus 15:17), that is, the specific place where God has decided that His people would live.

2. The word can mean the foundation or base on which something rests: that which supports and holds it in place. The psalmists sing that God "has founded the earth on its foundations" (Psalms 104:5), using an image that shows what everything relies on.

3. When speaking of God, the word designates His seat or residence from which He reigns. Several times, the text asks God to listen "from the place of your dwelling" (1 Kings 8:39; 2 Chronicles 6:30), that is, from heaven, His eternal throne.

4. In a sacred context, the word can refer to the sanctuary, the place consecrated to the divine presence and worship, as in 1 Kings 8:13 where Solomon dedicates the Temple, the earthly dwelling of God.

5. Sometimes the word is used for the earth itself, its surface or stable extent: that on which the inhabitants live and move every day.
H4349.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of fixing, establishing firmly. It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "to place" or "to set" something durably. The initial image is that of a solid base that is established and on which one builds: it is a place that cannot be moved, where everything is ordered and settled.
H4349.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms (where it often speaks of the divine seat), in the books of Kings and Chronicles (where it is used for the dwellings of the Temple and the king), and sometimes in the prophets. In passages related to the Temple, the word regularly designates heaven as the "place of the dwelling" of God, from where He hears prayers (1 Kings 8:39; 2 Chronicles 6:30). Elsewhere, it evokes an established residence or a place that has been prepared for a lasting presence (Exodus 15:17), or the solid foundation on which creation rests (Psalms 104:5). The word always carries a nuance of stability, order, and permanence.
H4349.portee: This word reminds the believer that God, although infinite and transcendent, has chosen places and moments to reveal Himself and meet His people: first the Temple, then the body of Christ, and ultimately the heart of the believer. It also emphasizes that the true stability of our lives rests solely on God, the only foundation that cannot be shaken. Knowing that God "from the place of His dwelling" observes all that happens on earth (Psalms 33:14) comforts the believer: no prayer is lost, no distress ignored.

sens: Fixed and solid base on which a heavy object rests
Supporting structure of a building or furniture
Foundation, stable support point
Figuratively: principle or element of stability
H4350.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the base or pedestal of stone or metal on which an object is placed to keep it stable and elevated. In Solomon's Temple, the king had ten bronze bases made to support the basins intended for water: each measured four cubits in length and width, with a structure featuring carved panels and wheels for mobility (1 Kings 7:27).
2. The word also applies to the supporting structure itself, the framework that receives and holds an object in place. The axles of the wheels of these bases were firmly attached to the structure (1 Kings 7:32), showing that the base was not just a passive pedestal but a true integrated construction.
3. In a more general sense, the word can evoke the foundation or support point that gives stability to the whole. All the bronze utensils of the Temple—columns, sea of bronze, bases, and others—together formed the fixed structure of the sanctuary (2 Kings 25:16).
4. Figuratively, the base becomes the principle or fundamental element on which something rests: the idea of stability, firmness, and solidity is at the heart of the word.
H4350.origine: The Hebrew word מְכוֹנָה (mekhoná) comes from the root כון (kun), which means "to establish, fix, prepare, make stable." This root appears in the creation of the world ("God established/founded the heavens") and in the general idea of arrangement, of thoughtful placement. The base is thus etymologically what has been "established" or "set in place" to create stability. The word also appears in the form מְכֻנָה (mekhunà) with a slight variation in vowel.
H4350.emploi: The word mékhoná appears 18 times in biblical Hebrew, almost exclusively in descriptions of Solomon's Temple and its utensils. The majority of uses (10) are found in 1 Kings 7, where it describes the ten bronze bases that Solomon had cast to support the basins of the Temple (1 Kings 7:27, 7:37, 7:43). The same word reappears when recounting the plundering or destruction of these bases by the Babylonians (2 Kings 25:16; Jeremiah 27:19; Jeremiah 52:20), showing that they were important and recognizable objects. The term rarely leaves this architectural and liturgical context of the Temple.
H4350.portee: This word reminds us that everything of value and dignity in the service of God—like the utensils of the Temple—rests on a solid and thoughtful foundation. Spiritually, it invites us to consider that our faith life itself needs a stable base: that of the Word of God and trust in Him. The word also emphasizes that the beauty and functionality of Israel's worship rested on durable material structures, testifying that God desires an orderly and lasting worship.

sens: The place where something or someone began, from where it comes
The country, the homeland from which one originates
The beginning, the root of what one is
H4351.detail: 1. The word refers to the geographical place, the land from which a person or people comes. Jerusalem comes from Canaan (Ezekiel 16:3): it is the land of its roots. 2. More broadly, it is the nation or homeland, the place where one has ties. The captive Egyptians must return "to the land of their origin" (Ezekiel 29:14), meaning Egypt, their homeland. 3. The word can also evoke the moment or circumstances of the beginning: "the place where you were created," God says to Jerusalem (Ezekiel 21:35), which is the starting point of its existence.
H4351.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to create" or "to shape." It is constructed with the notion of what is produced, made, or generated. The meaning naturally shifts from the verb "to create" to the noun "creation" and "what comes from it," hence "origin"—the result of the creative act, the beginning. It is mostly found in Ezekiel, who often speaks of the origins and roots of things.
H4351.emploi: The word appears only three times in biblical Hebrew, exclusively in the prophet Ezekiel, between chapters 16 and 29. Each time, it speaks of the origin of a city or a people: the origin of Jerusalem in Canaan, the place where it was created, and the country of origin of the Egyptians. It is a term that the prophet uses to root things in their history, to remind where peoples and cities come from. The context is always that of divine judgment: God brings His listeners back to their origins, to the moment they began.
H4351.portee: This word reminds us that everything we are has an origin, a beginning. For faith, this can mean that we are created, that we come from somewhere—from God. It also helps us understand that knowing our origins means knowing our spiritual and historical roots. In prophetic judgment, this implies that one cannot detach from their history: God confronts us with where we come from, to call us to responsibility.

sens: father of Gueuel, one of the twelve explorers sent to Canaan
H4352.detail: Maki is a man of Israel mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Gueuel, who was chosen among the twelve explorers sent by Moses to scout the land of Canaan before the people's entry (Numbers 13:15). Gueuel represented the tribe of Gad during this crucial mission.
H4352.origine: The name Maki literally means "diminution" or "decline" in Hebrew. It is a rare name in the Scriptures, borne by this one man from the Exodus generation.
H4352.emploi: Maki appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:15, where he is named as the father of Gueuel. This verse is part of the list of the twelve tribal leaders who were sent to explore Canaan for forty days. Although Maki himself is not described as part of the expedition, he is mentioned by his paternity, which shows the importance of genealogies in the biblical narrative of this period.

sens: son of Manasseh, ancestor of a great tribe
war chief and powerful man in Transjordan
founder of the descendants of Gilead
H4353G.detail:
1. Makir is the firstborn son of Manasseh, born of an Aramean concubine. He is the chief of an important branch of the tribe of Manasseh, and his descendants constitute a large family: Genesis 50:23 reports that Joseph saw the children of Makir to the third generation, which shows the importance of his lineage.
2. Makir is a man of war, a powerful military leader who controls the lands east of the Jordan. Joshua 17:1 specifies that he "had Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war," meaning that his military strength and prestige allowed him to acquire and conquer these territories.
3. Makir gives his name to his descendants, the Makirites, an important family that receives land as an inheritance. Numbers 32:40 shows that Moses officially gave him the region of Gilead for him to settle there with his descendants.
H4353G.origine: The name means "sold" in Hebrew. Makir is the son of Manasseh, one of the sons of Joseph. Through his mother, an Aramean woman, he belongs to both Israel and the Aramean culture of the ancient world. His descendants are called the Makirites, and they form an important tribal lineage.
H4353G.emploi: Makir primarily appears in genealogies and accounts of land distribution. He is first mentioned in Genesis 50:23 as the founder of a numerous lineage. He is then cited during the census and allocation of lands to the tribes (Numbers 26-27, 32 and Deuteronomy 3), where he receives the region of Gilead because of his status as a warrior. Judges 5:14 mentions him as a source of military leaders who join the fighters of Israel. Chronicles completes his genealogical story, detailing his children and descendants, which shows the lasting importance of his branch in the tribal history of Israel.
H4353G.portee: Makir illustrates how God distributes inheritance based on character and abilities: he receives the rich lands of Gilead because he is a capable warrior who can conquer and keep them. His story also shows that military strength and leadership are recognized and honored in God's covenant with Israel.

sens: Powerful chief of Transjordan who supported David
Son of Ammiel, resident of Lodebar
H4353H.detail: Makir is a high-ranking figure living during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He first appears in 2 Samuel 9:4-5 as the son of Ammiel, where King David sends to find Mephibosheth, the son of Saul, in Lodebar. Makir welcomes young Mephibosheth into his home and protects him. Later, in 2 Samuel 17:27, Makir is among the three great chiefs who come to supply David and his army during their flight from Absalom: he brings provisions to Mahanaim, demonstrating his influence and loyalty to the king. He is a man of power and resources in Transjordan, capable of playing a key role in decisive moments of King David's life.
H4353H.origine: The name Makir means "sold" in Hebrew, from a root that evokes a commercial transaction. It is the name of at least two figures in the Bible: the most famous is the eldest son of Manasseh (Genesis 50:23), progenitor of a large family; the biblical employment provided is a Transjordanian chief during David's time, a well-established historical figure in the accounts of the royal court.
H4353H.emploi: Makir appears three times in the accounts of David, always in connection with important moments. In 2 Samuel 9, he welcomes Mephibosheth, the surviving son of Saul, into his home, showing that he enjoyed great influence and sufficient resources to host a prince. In 2 Samuel 17, during Absalom's revolt, he is named among the three most powerful chiefs of the region (along with Shobi and Barzillai) who come to supply the fleeing king. His appearances in these two contexts reveal his status as a leading Transjordanian chief and his loyalty to the house of David.
H4353H.portee: Makir illustrates how God places powerful and generous men at key moments in the history of His people. His loyalty to David in exile shows that divine providence also operates through the discreet actions of wise leaders who support the king in times of trial. His example encourages the believer to see God's hand preparing support in times of crisis.

sens: descendants of the patriarch Machir
clan from the tribe of Manasseh
H4354.detail:
1. The Makirites are the descendants of the patriarch Machir, a man belonging to the tribe of Manasseh. Machir himself was born from a marriage between a man of the tribe of Manasseh and an Aramean woman, which shows how the peoples of the Levant intermingled at that time. By the time of the census described in the book of Numbers, this clan is already well established and bears the name of its ancestor.

2. The Makirites form a family or clan within the tribe of Manasseh. They appear in the census of the tribes of Israel as an identified group, indicating that they had land and a distinct role among the twelve tribes. The patronymic name "Makirites" shows how families were hierarchically structured: from Machir came Gilead, and from Gilead the Gileadites, thus forming distinct sub-groups.
H4354.origine: The word comes from the proper name Machir (מָכִיר), the founding patriarch of the clan. The root of the name Machir itself means "one who sells" or refers to commerce, although the meaning of the proper name is secondary. The formation "-ites" (in Hebrew -י) is the common patronymic suffix in Hebrew to designate members of a lineage: it is added to the name of the ancestor to form the collective name of the people or clan descending from it.
H4354.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Numbers during the great census of the second generation. It is in chapter 26, verse 29, that the Makirites are counted among the sons of Manasseh. This passage establishes the genealogical framework of the tribes before entering Canaan: each tribal clan is counted to determine the portion of territory that each will receive in the promised land. The Makirites, as descendants of Machir (whose son was Gilead), are an important element of this administrative and territorial structure of Israel.
H4354.portee: For the reader following the history of Israel, the Makirites embody the continuity of the genealogical line of God's people through the generations. Seeing a specific clan named in a census reminds us that God knows each of His children in detail, and that every family of His people has a place and a promise. This concrete mention also emphasizes how the promises made to Abraham unfold through tangible lineages and real territories.

sens: To fall, to collapse, to disappear
To be humiliated, lowered, unhappy
To be soft, negligent, lazy
H4355.detail:
1. To lower oneself primarily means to fall or physically collapse: this is what happens to the wicked in Job 24:24, when they "fall, they die like all men," suddenly reduced to nothing after having risen. The image is one of an irreversible fall.

2. The word also denotes moral humiliation, the state of one who is brought low by misfortune: the Israelites in Psalms 106:43 "became unhappy through their iniquity," meaning they were lowered, diminished, depressed by the consequences of their disobedience.

3. To lower oneself can finally mean to become soft, weak, without energy: in Ecclesiastes 10:18, when hands are lazy, the structure "collapses," loses its firmness, as if the building itself were softening and collapsing due to lack of maintenance.
H4355.origine: The Hebrew verb מָכַךְ (makhakh) evokes the idea of bending, curving, losing its stiffness. It is related to the image of something that no longer has the strength to stand upright. The root expresses the transition from a high or firm position to a low or soft position: this is why the word describes both physical falls and moral humiliation or weakening.
H4355.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always with a nuance of lowering or decay. In Job 24:24, it describes the sudden end of the wicked who collapse. In Psalms 106:43, it expresses the miserable state of the people defeated by their own sins. In Ecclesiastes 10:18, it depicts the house that deteriorates due to lack of maintenance. The three uses show how lowering oneself transitions from physical meaning (to fall, to collapse) to moral and domestic meaning (to be humiliated, to become negligent).
H4355.portee: This word reminds the reader that lowering oneself — whether through falling, humiliation, or laziness — is often the natural consequence of sin or neglect. It invites caution against negligence and lack of vigilance, which cause what has been built to collapse, just as iniquity lowers the one who commits it.

sens: Enclosure where sheep and goats are penned
Pasture where herds graze
Metaphorically, the people of God under the care of a shepherd
H4356.detail:
1. The sheepfold is primarily a building or enclosure where sheep and goats are kept to protect them at night or in case of danger. This is the image in Psalm 50:9, where God says to Israel: "I will not take a bull from your house, Nor goats from your sheepfolds" — He speaks of the enclosed animals, property of the people.
2. The word also refers to the pastures where herds graze during the day, the grassy lands where shepherds lead their flocks to feed. In Habakkuk 3:17, when the prophet cries that "the sheep will disappear from the pasture," he evokes the total absence of food for the livestock, the desolation of the grazing land.
3. In Psalm 78:70, where God "took David from the sheepfolds" to make him king, the word takes on a spiritual value: the sheepfold becomes the image of the humble condition of the people cared for by God, from which the anointed leader will emerge.
H4356.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to enclose" or "to confine." It specifically designates the enclosure or closed space where the flock is kept. This image of the protective enclosure resonates throughout the Bible in the ancient East, where livestock was both wealth, food, and the most precious possession of the shepherd or farmer. The sheepfold is the place where the animal is under guard, safe but also limited in its movements.
H4356.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It first designates the enclosure for sheep and goats (Psalms 50:9), then the pastures where they graze (Habakkuk 3:17). Its richest usage is in Psalm 78:70, where God chooses David "from the sheepfolds": the passage plays on the contrast between the humble condition of the shepherd of sheep and the royal charge that God confers upon him. The word remains close to the pastoral daily life of ancient Israelites, who raised flocks and kept them in enclosures or led them to graze.
H4356.portee: This word reminds us that God has chosen His shepherds from among the humblest. David, tending sheep, becomes king of Israel: it is a lesson on how God elevates the faithful from the most ordinary conditions. The sheepfold, a place of protection and care for the flock, also invites the believer to ask whether they trust God like the sheep trust their shepherd.

sens: State of what is complete, whole, lacking nothing
What is brought to its perfection, to its final accomplishment
Character of what reaches its full accomplishment
H4357.detail:
1. This word designates the state of a thing that is finished, complete, without defect or gap. In its unique biblical usage (2 Chronicles 4:21), it qualifies the "very" pure gold of the temple worship — gold that has reached its utmost refinement, devoid of any impurity or alteration.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of a perfection attained, of a work or state that has found its final accomplishment. It is the total absence of failure or lack.
H4357.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to finish," "to accomplish," "to perfect." It belongs to the family of verbs that express the idea of completion and absence of defect. In Hebrew, this type of noun constructed from an action root indicates the state or quality resulting from that action — here, the final result, the completed perfection.
H4357.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 4:21, where it describes the pure gold of Solomon's temple. In this context of worship and sanctuary, the term emphasizes the absolute quality of the materials reserved for divine service — gold brought to its maximum degree of purity. The unique and precise usage of this rare word shows that the Bible employs a very rich vocabulary to express nuances of quality and perfection.
H4357.portee: This word reminds us that the service rendered to God deserves the best, the purest, the most complete. The gold of the temple was not simply good — it was brought to perfection.
