For the believer, this evokes the call to give God a whole worship, without half-measures, and a heart that seeks integrity and completion in faith.

sens: with splendor and elegance in appearance
the state of what is complete and finished in its beauty
H4358.detail: 1. The word describes a sumptuous appearance, a particularly well-groomed and impressive presentation. It is the image of warriors or rulers dressed in luxury and distinction, whose entire equipment exudes power and refinement. In Ezekiel 23:12, the Assyrian governors are described as dressed "magnificently": the image emphasizes their presence and imposing appearance that attracted admiration. 2. The deeper meaning denotes perfection, the complete accomplishment of a beauty or excellence without defect. It is the idea that something or someone reaches its completion and total splendor, without lack. In Ezekiel 38:4, the word applies to an entire army dressed with this same perfection of equipment, suggesting a fully organized and impressive war machine.
H4358.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to complete" or "to accomplish." It is related to the idea of totality and finishing: something that is fully realized, that has no cracks or lacks. In biblical Hebrew, this family of words always evokes the idea of a beauty or excellence brought to its conclusion, without defect.
H4358.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Ezekiel, and always to describe a clothing or warrior appearance. In Ezekiel 23:12, it characterizes the Assyrian leaders who attract attention by their luxurious attire. In Ezekiel 38:4, it applies to Gog's army equipped in a complete and impressive manner. In both cases, the context is one of an external appearance that manifests power, wealth, and perfect order. The word never speaks of moral or spiritual beauty, but always of visible and material splendor.
H4358.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible sees external beauty and order, but judges them in light of the heart and intention. The "magnificently" dressed warriors and rulers of Ezekiel attract by their appearance, but the prophetic context makes them figures of seduction and carnal power, not true strength. For the believer, this teaches not to confuse external splendor with true spiritual excellence.

sens: Character of what is complete, without defect or lack
State of total accomplishment
Beauty or excellence achieved
H4359.detail:
1. The word first designates what is entirely complete, without any missing or defective part. It is the idea of a totality that leaves nothing to be desired. In Psalms 50:2, "the perfect beauty" of Zion expresses its total accomplishment, the consummate harmony of the holy City.
2. More broadly, it is the state of a thing or a person that has reached its final and completed form, without defect. This can concern a finished work, a flawless beauty, or the fullness of something.
H4359.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root כלל (khall), which means "to complete, to finish, to accomplish." This root evokes the idea of gathering and finishing, arriving at the end of something to make it a whole. Words of the same family express the idea of wholeness, totality, or completeness. The word carries the image of a work that reaches its end and becomes whole.
H4359.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 50:2. It is used to qualify the beauty of Zion, the holy mountain from which God shines. It is a quality attributed to the holy place par excellence, emphasizing its absolute and flawless character. Its uniqueness in the Bible makes it a carefully chosen term by the psalmist to express supreme excellence.
H4359.portee: This word reminds us that God chooses for His dwelling a place of perfection and absolute beauty. It invites the believer to contemplate the completeness and harmony of divine creation, and to desire in their heart this integrity that can only be found in the presence of God.

sens: A garment or fabric crafted with care, of high quality
A collection of precious and well-made items
That which is complete, perfect, without flaw
H4360.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a luxury garment or fabric, made with artistry and refinement. In Ezekiel 27:24, it refers to magnificent garments exchanged in the markets of Tyre, embroideries and richly crafted fabrics, reflecting the care taken in their creation.
2. More broadly, the word can denote any collection of precious and refined objects, high-value goods assembled with order and beauty. It is an image of wealth and material perfection.
3. The deeper meaning of the word is that of completeness and perfection: something that has been finished, finalized, brought to its conclusion with excellence. It evokes the idea that nothing is lacking, that everything is in place.
H4360.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to accomplish, to make complete." It is related to the idea of perfection and completion. The prefix forms a noun designating the resulting object: that which has been made perfect, that which bears the mark of accomplishment. This is why it fits so well with precious garments, which are the culmination of the work of the weaver and the embroiderer.
H4360.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:24. It is part of the grand enumeration of goods that merchants brought to Tyre, the famous Phoenician city of maritime trade. The context is that of Tyre's fabulous wealth, listed before its prophesied downfall. The beautiful goods mentioned—blue-dyed cloaks, embroideries, rich fabrics—illustrate the luxury and artistry of ancient civilizations, and the material prosperity that the Bible highlights as fragile.
H4360.portee: This word reminds us that beauty and excellence in human work are a reality in the Bible. It is neither despised nor overly glorified, but observed as a sign of the talents that God has given to men. However, the context of Ezekiel 27 also warns us that material wealth, however beautiful, is perishable and cannot be the foundation of our security or hope.

sens: That which nourishes, that which serves for sustenance
Regular supply of food intended to feed someone or a group
H4361.detail:
1. That which nourishes, that which serves for sustenance: the word concretely refers to the food or provisions necessary for living. In 1 Kings 5:11, Solomon provides Hiram with wheat and olive oil as provisions for his household, that is, to feed his household.
2. Regular supply of food intended to feed someone or a group: this is not a simple one-time ration, but a continuous and organized supply. The expression "every year" in the same verse shows that it is an ordinary and permanent charge that the king must assume to meet the needs of the court or administration.
H4361.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root כול (koul), which means "to sustain, to nourish, to maintain." The form makkólet is a nominal derivative that concretely designates that by which one supports someone: the food and provisions necessary for their existence. This root expresses the idea of support and continuity.
H4361.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 5:11, where it describes the food allocation that Solomon provides to Hiram, king of Tyre, in exchange for cedar wood for the construction of the Temple. This royal and administrative context shows that "provision" applies to a regular and official supply of food intended to sustain the court or the administration of a great person. The term thus emphasizes not only the food itself but the duty to ensure its continuous supply.
H4361.portee: This word reminds us that providing for the food of others is a real responsibility, inscribed in the relationships of power and alliance between men. It also shows that even at the level of great kings, life depends on the regular supply of bread and oil—simple yet essential goods. It is an invitation to recognize that daily sustenance is a serious matter, whether given or received.

sens: Precious riches kept safe and hidden
Material resources reserved, accumulated, and protected
H4362.detail:
1. The word refers to riches—gold, silver, precious objects—that are hidden or set aside for protection. In Daniel 11:43, the conquering king "takes possession of the treasures of gold and silver" of Egypt: these are the hidden or carefully guarded reserves that he plunders during his victory.
2. More broadly, it refers to any precious resource accumulated and kept safe—not exposed for all to see, but carefully preserved as a reserve. The idea of secrecy or protection is at the heart of the word.
H4362.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of hiding or keeping hidden. It fundamentally designates that which is concealed from view, buried or kept secret. The nominal form expresses the entirety of things thus hidden or reserved, notably the riches that one accumulates and protects.
H4362.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 11:43. In this context of political prophecy, it describes the riches of the kingdom of Egypt—the royal treasures, the reserves of gold and silver—that the king of the North will conquer and appropriate. It is a purely concrete and material usage, without spiritual figure or extension.
H4362.portee: This word reminds us that earthly riches, however well guarded and hidden they may be, remain exposed to plunder and loss. It invites the believer not to place their trust in the treasures of this world, but in that which cannot be taken away.

sens: City of Benjamin
Strategic position in ancient Israel
Site of confrontation between Saul and the Philistines
H4363.detail:
1. Michmas is a city located in the mountainous region of Benjamin, about 16 kilometers north of Jerusalem, near Ramah. Its name means "hidden," probably referring to its steep and remote position. It corresponds to the modern village of Mukhmas.
2. The city occupied a strategic military position, notably at the passage of a heavily defended mountain. This is why it became a point of contention in the battles between Israel and the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:5).
3. Michmas is best known as the site of the campaign led by King Saul and his son Jonathan against the Philistines, around 1020 B.C. (1 Samuel 13:2). Jonathan displays remarkable courage by attacking an enemy outpost.
H4363.origine: The Hebrew name מִכְמָס (mikhmas) literally means "hidden" or "concealed," suggesting the geographical nature of the place: a locality not easily visible, hidden in rocky slopes. This name reflects the mountainous and difficult-to-access character of this region of Benjamin.
H4363.emploi: Michmas is primarily mentioned in the story of Saul and Jonathan against the Philistines (1 Samuel 13-14). It is at Michmas that the Philistines set up camp before the battle (1 Samuel 13:5), and it is near Michmas that Jonathan achieves a spectacular victory (1 Samuel 13:23, 14:5, 14:31). The city reappears later in the Old Testament during the return from exile (Ezra 2:27, Nehemiah 7:31, 11:31) and in Isaiah's prophecy regarding the Assyrian invasion (Isaiah 10:28), where it is listed among the threatened cities on the way to Jerusalem.

sens: Mesh of cords or intertwined threads used to catch game or fish
Figuratively, a trap or danger that ensnares
H4364A.detail:
1. A net is a work of cords or threads woven to form meshes. It is used to catch game or fish. In Isaiah 51:20, the children of Jerusalem are compared to a deer fallen into a net: they lie in the streets, caught in misfortune like a creature trapped.
2. The word also figuratively denotes an invisible trap, a situation that ensnares and paralyzes. The net then represents a hidden danger that confines the one caught in it, deprived of freedom and means of escape.
H4364A.origine: The Hebrew word מִכְמָר (mikh.mar) comes from a root that evokes weaving and intertwining. It concretely designates a woven net, that is, a set of intertwined meshes intended to capture. The image of the net, common in the Bible, easily transitions from the concrete sense (fishing or hunting tool) to the figurative sense (moral trap or danger).
H4364A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Isaiah 51:20. It is used in a poetic image where the children of Israel, exhausted and failing, are compared to a deer caught in a net. This comparison expresses total helplessness and imprisonment in misfortune: just as an animal cannot escape from a net, the people find themselves without resources in the face of God's anger.
H4364A.portee: This image of the net reminds the believer that sin and judgment act as traps that immobilize us and take away all freedom. It invites us to recognize our need for deliverance and to seek in God the one who alone can free us from what binds us.

sens: trap set to capture
spiritual snare or deception
H4364B.detail:
1. The net is a woven device, set to catch animals or fish — this is the simplest and most concrete image of the word. In Psalm 141:10, the poet asks that the wicked fall into their own nets, meaning that they be caught in their own plots.
2. By extension, a net denotes any snare or deception: the invisible danger set by an adversary. The image evokes both the capture of a beast and, spiritually, the captivity of sin or evil.
H4364B.origine: The word makh.mor is a variant of the word mikh.mar (H4364A): both come from the root kmr which means "to tie," "to weave." The net is therefore fundamentally a weaving, a knotted fabric meant to hold. In Hebrew, several words designate traps and nets according to their shape or use: the word retained here emphasizes the aspect of tight weaving and intertwining.
H4364B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 141:10. It is a prayer of the psalmist asking the Lord that the wicked who threaten him — those who set traps for him — fall into their own nets. The image of the net is common in the Psalms to describe the dangers and plots of enemies: it is a call for God's justice to turn the trap against the one who set it.
H4364B.portee: This image of the net turned back on the one who set it teaches a profound lesson: he who seeks to ensnare others through deception or sin risks being captured by his own plans. For the believer, this reminds us that divine justice does not leave malice unpunished, and that asking God to intervene also means entrusting Him with our protection against the snares of evil.

sens: Fishing net, with which fish are caught
Means of capture or trap, in a figurative sense
H4365A.detail:
1. A fishing net is a woven or braided device thrown into the water to catch fish. In Habakkuk 1:15, the prophet describes a war chief who "draws" nations "into his net" like a fisherman captures his prey — this is the concrete image of the word.
2. Figuratively, the net becomes a trap or an instrument of domination: the one who uses it captures and enslaves. The fishermen in Habakkuk 1:15-16 even sacrifice to their nets, worshiping their own power of capture, so intoxicating is the wealth it brings them. The net symbolizes here an irresistible force that renders powerless those who fall into it.
H4365A.origine: The Hebrew word מִכְמֶרֶת comes from a root evoking the action of "weaving" or "braiding." It is a manufactured instrument, constructed of intertwined meshes to hold what attempts to escape. The family of the word designates all kinds of nets or traps set — it is common vocabulary in the Eastern Mediterranean where fishing was a daily practiced art.
H4365A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, in verses 15 and 16 of chapter 1 of Habakkuk. The prophet denounces the Chaldean (Babylonian) Empire by comparing it to a fisherman who "draws nations into his net." The repetition of the word ("net" and "rets") in these two verses emphasizes the conqueror's obsession with his instrument of power: he sacrifices to it, offers incense to it, finds his glory and wealth in it. It is a sarcastic portrait: the Chaldean fishermen worship their own technology of domination as a god.
H4365A.portee: This passage invites the reader to recognize how human power — political, military, economic — functions like a net: it captures, it holds, it enslaves. Habakkuk shows us that those who build their pride on the domination of others are ultimately blind to their own powerlessness before God. For the believer, this word reminds us that only God masters destinies; to wish to reign like a Babylonian conqueror is to bow before a false god.

sens: Fishing net, lattice of knotted cords to catch fish
Network or trap set to catch
H4365B.detail:
1. The net is a lattice of cords or threads knotted in tight meshes, thrown or spread over water to catch fish. The word first evokes the concrete tool of the fisherman: in Isaiah 19:8, the fishermen who "spread nets on the waters" see their trade ruined.
2. Figuratively, the net denotes anything that confines, traps, or leads to death — a trap set, a network that captures. This image of capture is frequent in biblical poetry to speak of danger or God's judgment.
H4365B.origine: The Hebrew word מִכְמֶרֶת (mikhmèret) comes from a root meaning "to weave" or "to knot": it literally designates what is knotted together. It is a technical term in the vocabulary of fishing, well attested in the Old Testament for the concrete tool of the fisherman.
H4365B.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved Bible, in Isaiah 19:8. It is part of a prophecy against Egypt: the Lord announces that the flooding of the Nile will cease, and the waters will dry up. The fishermen, who depended on the Nile, will be ruined — whether they cast a hook or spread their nets, all their work will become barren. The net here is simply the instrument of their trade, but it also symbolizes their anxiety and loss in the face of God's judgment.
H4365B.portee: This word reminds us that God controls even the means of livelihood that we believe are secure. For the believer, it also invites us to meditate on the biblical image of the net: our own traps can turn against us, but God alone holds the net of history and judgment.

sens: City or locality on the border in northern Ephraim
Geographical reference point between Ephraim and Manasseh
H4366.detail:
1. Micmethath is a city or locality mentioned in the account of the division of the Promised Land among the tribes of Israel. It was located in the northern region of Ephraim, near Shechem, serving as an important landmark for delineating the territories of the different tribes (Joshua 17:7).
2. This place marked a transition point between the territory of Ephraim and that of Manasseh. It appears at the borders, first on the western side of Ephraim and then within the boundaries of Manasseh, making it a passageway or junction area between two tribal territories (Joshua 16:6 and 17:7).
H4366.origine: The name Micmethath literally means "hiding place" or "hidden place," possibly evoking a secluded or sheltered position in the mountainous terrain of this region in central Canaan. This Hebrew name reflects the topographical features of the Promised Land.
H4366.emploi: Micmethath appears only twice in the Bible, both in the context of the territorial division of Israel in the book of Joshua. It is first mentioned as the western boundary of the territory of Ephraim (Joshua 16:6), and then as a reference point in the delineation of the territory of Manasseh (Joshua 17:7). These two mentions show that this locality served as a fixed landmark for geographers and administrators of ancient Israel, allowing for precise definitions of the borders between tribes.

sens: A man from the Jewish community during the time of exile and return
H4367.detail: Macnadbaï is one of the sons of Bani who, upon returning from exile under Ezra, ended his marriage to a foreign woman, thus obeying the command of the prophet Ezra to preserve the purity of the restored community (Ezra 10:40).
H4367.origine: The Hebrew name מַכְנַדְבַי (Macnadbaï) literally means "he has humbled my willing ones" or "he has made humble my willing people." It is a theophoric name where the implied divine subject guides the action. The name reflects a piety oriented towards humility before God.
H4367.emploi: Macnadbaï appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:40, in the list of men from Judah and Benjamin who took foreign wives and divorced them at Ezra's command. He is part of the family of Bani, one of the prominent houses that participated in this religious reformation after the return from exile. This unique mention situates him in a decisive moment in Israel's history: the reconstruction of the religious identity of the people.

sens: City of Judah inhabited after the exile
Place of residence for the Judeans who returned from captivity
H4368.detail: Mecona is a small city in Judah that was repopulated after the return from exile of the Judeans to Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:28). It appears in the list of localities where the inhabitants of Judah resettled, alongside other cities like Ziklag. Its name literally means "foundation," possibly evoking a city established on solid bases or rebuilt after devastation.
H4368.origine: The Hebrew name מְכֹנָה (mekhonah) derives from the root כון (koun), which means "to establish" or "to found." This name reflects the idea of a stable base or a solidly established construction. It is a typical geographical proper name from the region of Judah, designating a locality whose importance lies primarily in its reoccupation after the Babylonian exile.
H4368.emploi: Mecona appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:28, in the context of the repopulation of Judah after the return from captivity. It is among the cities that the children of Judah and Benjamin inhabited again, according to the genealogical records of the time of Nehemiah. This mention is part of the narrative of the restoration of Israel and the demographic stabilization of the Judean territory after the Babylonian exile.

sens: place where one rests, where something is placed
base, foundation on which an object rests
H4369.detail:
1. The word first designates a place where someone or something rests — a stable residence or deposit location. In Zechariah 5:11, the Ephah (a symbolic basket containing wickedness) will have its "place": a fixed location where it will be established, like a dwelling.
2. By extension, it is also the base, the pedestal on which a construction or object finds its stability. The word evokes the image of a solid support, a foundation.
H4369.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "to fix" or "to establish." It is a variant of מְכוֹנָה (mékhonah, H4350), which carries the same meaning. This family of words designates what is established, installed durably — something or someone that has found its place, its final rest.
H4369.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zechariah 5:11. In this visionary passage, the angel explains to Zechariah that the Ephah (symbol of iniquity) will have its "place," meaning a fixed and established location in the land of Shinar (ancient Babylon). The usage emphasizes the idea that even wickedness will find rest, a defined installation — which prepares for the end times.
H4369.portee: This word reminds us that everything, in the divine order, finds its place and rest. For the believer, it evokes the promise that God establishes the order of things according to His will, and that history concludes according to His sovereign plan.

sens: Linen garment worn under the tunic by Hebrew priests
Piece of fabric intended to cover the body's nakedness
Undergarment prescribed in worship to preserve dignity and holiness
H4370.detail:
1. The linen undergarment is primarily a ritual undergarment: a linen garment that priests must wear under their sacred tunic, covering the lower body "from the loins to the thighs" (Exodus 28:42). It is a practical textile piece, woven or twisted, that is an integral part of the priestly attire alongside the turban and belt (Leviticus 16:4).
2. Beyond the clothing aspect, the undergarment represents the covering of nakedness: it preserves the priest's decency at the altar, especially when he bends to offer sacrifices or remove the ashes from the burnt offering (Leviticus 6:3). This covering is not accessory—it is part of the respect due to the sacred nature of divine service.
3. Finally, the undergarment embodies a requirement of ritual holiness: worn of white linen (symbol of purity), according to precise prescriptions, it signifies that one approaching God must not excite sweat nor transgress the rules that mark the separation between the profane and the sacred (Ezekiel 44:18).
H4370.origine: The Hebrew word מִכְנָס (mikh.nas) comes from a root meaning "to cover" or "to clothe." Its etymology evokes the idea of "that which envelops" or "that which conceals." This technical term of priestly vocabulary appears only in the legal texts concerning Israelite worship, where the garment holds major theological importance.
H4370.emploi: This word appears only five times in the Bible, always to designate the same ritual undergarment imposed on the priests. It is found in Leviticus and in the narrative or legislative parts related to the Tabernacle and the Temple: Exodus 28 and 39 (instructions for making the priestly garment), Leviticus 6 and 16 (prescriptions for daily service and the Day of Atonement), and Ezekiel 44 (norm for future priests of the restored Temple). Each usage reinforces the idea that this garment is not a freedom but a strict obligation, integrated into the rules of purity and decorum that govern worship.
H4370.portee: For today's believer, the priestly undergarment reminds us of a truth often forgotten: access to God is not done just any way, nor dressed just any way. The details of the priestly attire teach that our approach to God requires respect, preparation, and decency. The Epistle to the Hebrews transposes this lesson: under the New Covenant, all believers have become "priests," and we are called to present ourselves before God with reverence, pure hearts, and clean hands.

sens: A portion taken from a spoil or possession and reserved for the Lord
A proportion or quota established according to a calculation rule
An offering given to God in recognition of His sovereignty
H4371.detail:
1. In the passages from Numbers 31, the tithe refers to the portion of the war booty that the Israelite soldiers must set aside for the service of the tabernacle. It is a mandatory deduction: from each group of 500 men, oxen, donkeys, or sheep, one animal or one person is chosen as the tithe (Numbers 31:28). The word evokes a tithe of the spoil, a tribute to God.
2. The tithe follows a fixed and calculated proportion: it is a determined fraction (one out of five hundred) that must be taken equally from each category of spoil. Moses applies this rule precisely: 675 people for the tithe, 72 oxen, 61 donkeys, 32 sheep (Numbers 31:37-40).
3. This reserved portion becomes a holy offering given to the priest Eleazar for the service of the Lord. The tithe acknowledges that God is the master of the spoil and that a portion belongs to Him before any sharing among the soldiers (Numbers 31:41).
H4371.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of setting aside or separating a portion. It originally designates a calculated portion taken according to a precise rule. The image is one of sharing: a line is drawn, and it is said, "this belongs to the Lord." It is an administrative and religious term that evokes both calculation and obligation toward God.
H4371.emploi: The word appears only in chapter 31 of the book of Numbers, in six consecutive verses all dealing with the same event: after the victory against Midian, Moses establishes how to share the spoil. The tithe is the divine portion, distinguished from the rest of the spoil that the soldiers share. It is a mandatory tribute, not freely offered, but imposed by law: each must give a portion. The context shows that the tithe sanctifies the spoil by acknowledging God's right over it.
H4371.portee: For the believer, the tithe teaches that all spoil, all gain, all victory belongs first to God. Giving God a portion of the fruit of our labors is not an option, but an act of recognition that all comes from His hand. It invites the Christian to reflect on the place they reserve for God in their resources and successes.

sens: that which covers something to protect or hide it
canvas or skin stretched to cover a structure
set of skins or canvases that form the outer envelope of a tent or building
H4372.detail: 1. In the simplest sense, a covering is that which covers something to protect it or keep it safe. Noah removed the covering of the ark to look outside and see that the water had dried (Genesis 8:13): the word here refers to the roof or lid that closed the great vessel. 2. For the tabernacle, the covering is a canvas or skin that is stretched over the structure to protect it from the elements. Exodus 39:34 mentions two overlapping coverings: one of dyed ram skins, and one of dolphin skins on top, thus forming a waterproof envelope. 3. The word also designates the entire set of protective elements in the context of transporting or assembling the portable sanctuary: sacred objects are wrapped to preserve them during the journey (Numbers 4:10, 4:12).
H4372.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to cover" or "to hide." It literally designates that which extends over something to veil or protect it. This image of covering and protection is central in the vocabulary of the tabernacle, where care is taken to cover every sacred object and structure to keep them safe from the profane and from sight.
H4372.emploi: This word appears about a dozen times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of the flood (Genesis 8:13) and especially in the chapters on the tabernacle (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers). It first refers to the roof of the ark, then becomes a technical term for the skins or canvases that form the protective envelope of the tabernacle and its accessories. In the context of worship, it holds particular importance: the coverings are not mere ornaments, but functional elements that separate the sacred from the profane and preserve the integrity of the worship objects during transport (Numbers 3:25, 4:8, 4:12).
H4372.portee: This notion of protective covering reminds the believer that true worship emphasizes the separation between the holy and the profane. The coverings of the tabernacle symbolize the divine protection that envelops His people and sacred places. Today, it invites reflection on how we preserve and respect what is consecrated to God.

sens: Quantity of counted people or things
Estimated value of a thing
H4373.detail:
1. The number is the quantity obtained by counting people or objects. In Exodus 12:4, the number of people in a house is calculated to determine how to share the Passover lamb: each will eat according to what they can consume, and the count is made person by person.
2. The number can also designate the value or estimated price of a thing. In Leviticus 27:23, the priest evaluates and sets the price of a field dedicated to God according to an estimate until the year of Jubilee: it is to establish the number or value of what is offered.
H4373.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to count" or "to calculate." It designates the action of enumerating and its result: the count, the quantity. The same family of words produces verbs and nouns related to enumeration and estimation of goods.
H4373.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 12:4, it concerns the counting of people to share the Passover lamb equitably. In Leviticus 27:23, it occurs in the context of vows and dedications to the Lord, where the priest must evaluate the value of the offered goods. The meaning shifts between "count" and "value" depending on whether one is enumerating objects or estimating their price.
H4373.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and knows the details of His people and their possessions: there is precision in divine ordinances. It also calls for responsibility and honesty in our estimates and commitments to God.

sens: That which covers something, hides it or protects it
The fat that envelops the internal organs of an animal
A garment or something that wraps around the body
A drapery or fabric that adorns a space
H4374.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning: it is everything that covers or envelops something else. In Leviticus 9:19, it is the fat that covers the entrails of the sacrificed ram — a natural covering that protects the organs.
2. In the imagery of the abode of the dead in Isaiah 14:11, worms become the "covering" of the fallen king: a dark image where what once adorned him with glory now covers him with decay.
3. The word also refers to clothing in a broad sense — everything that dresses the body and distinguishes it socially. In Isaiah 23:18, impure gains will finance magnificent "garments" to serve the Lord: the fabric becomes a sign of dignity and consecration.
4. A drapery or decorative fabric that adorns a building. In Ezekiel 27:7, the ship of Tyre is adorned with "draperies" of embroidered linen: the word rises to the sense of lavish decoration that honors the structure.
H4374.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cover." It is a noun formed to designate the action of covering that has become an object — that which covers is itself a covering. This root appears in many biblical contexts where it is about protecting, hiding, or adorning, and the word naturally unfolds from the concrete (the physical envelope) to the abstract (the decor, the garment of status).
H4374.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the prophetic and ritual books. In Leviticus, it is a very precise anatomical term for the sacrifice. In Isaiah and Ezekiel, it enriches: on one hand, an image of death and shame (the worms cover the corpse of the king), on the other hand, a symbol of wealth and splendor (the fine fabrics that clothe merchant ships or the servants of God). The word thus oscillates between what protects and what dehumanizes, between the dignity of clothing and the derision of decomposition.
H4374.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate both the order of creation — the fat that protects the organs — and the vanity of earthly glory, which ends up under the worms. It also illustrates how goods and riches, consecrated to the Lord, become a source of true dignity. It is a humble word that speaks of the fragility of the body and the great dignity of serving God.

sens: Burial cave near Hebron where the patriarchs were buried
Field containing this cave, purchased by Abraham from Ephron the Hittite
H4375.detail:
1. Machpelah is the name of a burial cave located near Hebron, in the land of Canaan. It is where Abraham buried his wife Sarah (Genesis 23:19), and where Isaac, Jacob, and other members of the patriarchal family were later buried (Genesis 25:9; Genesis 50:13). This cave has taken on crucial importance for the patriarchs: it represented their territorial anchorage in the promised land and the sign of the divine promise.
2. The term also refers to the entire field surrounding this cave. Abraham purchased it from Ephron the Hittite as a "burial property" (Genesis 23:17), which means he was now the perpetual owner for burying his descendants. This field-cave thus became the first real estate owned by Abraham in Canaan.
H4375.origine: The Hebrew name Machpelah literally means "double" or "double portion." It may refer to the double structure of the burial site (a cave with multiple chambers) or to a field divided into two parcels. It is an ancient geographical name, attested as early as the first narratives of Genesis.
H4375.emploi: Machpelah appears 6 times in the Bible, exclusively in Genesis, during the account of Abraham's purchase of the field (Genesis 23) and in passages relating to the burials of the patriarchs (Genesis 25:9; Genesis 49:30; Genesis 50:13). Each mention emphasizes the importance of this place as a legitimate burial site and family property in the land of Canaan. The accompanying terms vary slightly ("cave of the field," "field"), but always refer to this same strategic and sacred location.
H4375.portee: Machpelah symbolizes for biblical faith the rooting of the chosen people in the promised land. It is the first real estate that Abraham possesses in Canaan, not by conquest but by purchase and covenant. This place reminds us that divine promises are inscribed in a concrete history, a land, a succession of faithful generations. For the believer, it is also an image of permanence and the spiritual inheritance passed from father to son.

sens: Exchange a good or service for money or compensation
Alienate a right or inheritance
Deliver someone to a power or fate, abandon them
Place a person in servitude
H4376.detail:
1. To sell primarily means to transfer an object in exchange for money or value: Jacob sells his birthright to Esau (Genesis 25:33), and a man can sell a live ox after an accident (Exodus 21:35). It is the simplest commercial exchange.

2. The word also refers to the alienation of a right or property: the sale of a house or land (Leviticus 25:14-16), or the sale of a daughter into servitude by her father (Exodus 21:7). It is a legal act that transfers possession.

3. In a more serious sense, to sell means to deliver someone to an enemy or to death: God says He has "sold" Israel to the peoples who dominate it (Deuteronomy 32:30), or that the children of Israel have been "sold" to the nations in captivity (Isaiah 52:3). The image is one of delivery without recourse, like a slave.

4. Finally, the word describes the enslavement of a person: an Israelite sold into slavery can only be for a limited time (Leviticus 25:42), while a child sold by his father or captured in war becomes a slave (Exodus 21:16). It is the loss of freedom.
H4376.origine: The verb to sell comes from an ancient Hebrew root that evokes the idea of ceding or transferring for payment. In the Old Testament, this verb is used for all types of transactions: ordinary sales of goods, but also the alienation of rights or the delivery of people. The underlying image is always that of an exchange that transfers something to a third party, often in a definitive manner or against one's will.
H4376.emploi: The verb to sell appears 74 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Torah (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the historical books. It is first used for ordinary transactions: sale of goods, land, livestock. But the Bible regularly extends it to more serious realities: the sale of a person into slavery, especially for debt (Leviticus 25), or the delivery of Israel to its enemies by divine judgment (Judges 2:14; Judges 3:8; Deuteronomy 32:30). The context often reveals a rupture or betrayal: Joseph's brothers sell him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:27-28), and Nehemiah condemns those who want to sell their brothers to the nations (Nehemiah 5:8). The theological use of the word shows that God "delivers" His people to judgment when He abandons them due to unfaithfulness.
H4376.portee: The word to sell reminds the believer that everything he possesses — his goods, his rights, even his freedom — only belongs to him in trust. The Old Testament strictly frames the sale of Hebrew slaves to remind that no one is to be sold permanently (Leviticus 25:42). The theological meaning of the word also invites reflection on the danger of abandoning God or His word: it is to "sell" oneself to sin and condemnation. Redemption by God then becomes the only hope in the face of this fatal sale.

sens: market value of a thing, what one can obtain by exchanging or selling it
sum of money paid to obtain or use something
rarity and excellence of a person or thing
H4377.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes what a commodity is worth on the market. In Nehemiah 13:16, the Tyrians sell fish and various goods: the word "goods" literally translates what is brought for exchange or sale. 2. It can also refer to the amount one must pay for something. To the children of Israel who ask to cross the land of the king of Edom, the response concerns the price of water (Numbers 20:19): it is the agreed sum in exchange. 3. By extension, this word expresses intrinsic value, the precious quality of a person or thing. The virtuous woman in Proverbs 31:10 is worth more than rubies: this is not a market price, but her moral and rare excellence.
H4377.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of separating, distinguishing, or valuing. From this, the meaning of "what has value" or "what deserves to be paid" naturally arises. The word belongs to the family of those that speak of exchange and evaluation in the economic and social life of Israel.
H4377.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament. In Numbers 20:19, it concerns the price of water to be paid to the king of Edom. In Nehemiah 13:16, it designates the goods brought by the Tyrian merchants, which was a scandal since they sold them on the Sabbath. In Proverbs 31:10, it expresses the priceless value of a virtuous woman. The word thus circulates between three contexts: everyday economy (payment, goods), and the evaluation of what is truly precious in the eyes of God.
H4377.portee: This word invites the believer to distinguish between the price of visible things and the true moral and spiritual value. The virtuous woman costs more than rubies not in silver, but in excellence of heart: it reminds us that God values what cannot be sold on the market. The Sabbath, too, has a price — it should not be transgressed for commerce. This word soberly teaches the hierarchy of values.

sens: person one knows
friend, close one
someone with whom one has a familiar relationship
H4378.detail: 1. The word designates a person one knows, someone with whom one has an established personal relationship. In the context of 2 Kings 12:5-7, the priests were to collect money from those they knew — that is, from the faithful they personally knew — for the repairs of the temple. This was not an anonymous collection, but a direct request addressed to people from their familiar circle. 2. More broadly, it is a relationship of closeness and trust: a friend or close one with whom one maintains regular ties, not a mere stranger. The word implies a certain familiarity and a shared history.
H4378.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root יכר (y-k-r), which means "to know" or "to recognize." This root expresses the idea of knowing someone by sight, identifying them, and having an established relationship with them. The form makkar thus literally denotes "the one who is known," that is, the known person, or by extension, someone with whom one has established knowledge.
H4378.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, only in 2 Kings 12, during the account of the collection of money for the temple repairs. In this context, the priests were to first collect money from their acquaintances (verse 5), that is, from the faithful with whom they had personal relationships. But King Joash, considering that this method was not effective — the collected money was to serve the repairs and not enrich the priests — orders the priests to cease this practice and to directly hand over the money for the temple repairs (verse 7). The word here marks the idea of a familiarity exploited for personal gain.
H4378.portee: This passage highlights a tension between personal relationships and faithfulness to the house of God. The priests had ties with the faithful, but these ties should not divert generosity from the sacred purpose: the maintenance of the sanctuary. For the Christian, this reminds us that our acquaintances and friends should help us serve God with integrity, not serve ourselves.

sens: Excavation dug in the ground to extract salt
Arid and barren place, covered with thorns, abandoned to desolation
H4379.detail: 1. A salt mine is an excavation, a quarry dug in the ground to extract salt. It is a place of work and exploitation, often arid and unwelcoming. In Zephaniah 2:9, the salt mine literally describes a mining extraction area. 2. Figuratively, the term becomes a symbol of desolation and absolute sterility. When the prophet says that Moab and Ammon will become "a salt mine," he is not only describing a quarry but a landscape of ruins: unproductive land, covered with thorns, abandoned. It is the very image of divine curse — a place where nothing grows anymore, where life has withdrawn (Zephaniah 2:9).
H4379.origine: The Hebrew word mikh­reh comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or boring. It primarily designates the excavation itself, the hole dug to extract a resource. Salt, a white mineral that crystallizes and accumulates naturally near certain lakes and seas, was a valuable resource in the ancient East, used both for food preservation and as a medium of exchange. A salt mine is thus both a place of potential wealth and a hostile environment for life.
H4379.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zephaniah 2:9. The prophet uses it to announce divine judgment on Moab and Ammon. These two nations, enemies of Israel, will be reduced to the state of salt mines — that is, to ravaged, infertile land where no life flourishes anymore. It is an image of total and irreversible destruction, where punishment is expressed through abandonment and desolation.
H4379.portee: For the reader, this striking image of divine judgment reminds us that the destruction of rebellious nations is complete and that God leaves nothing standing of those who oppose Him. It also shows the certainty of prophetic word: what is announced as ruin comes to pass. It is a solemn warning about the consequences of rejecting the God of Israel.

sens: offensive white weapon, sword or saber
instrument of violence and destruction
symbol of military strength or judgment
H4380.detail:
1. The sword is a sharp weapon, a sword or saber used in close combat. In Genesis 49:5, Jacob speaks of the "swords" of Simeon and Levi to evoke their violent temperament and their ability to wage war.
2. The word also refers to the instrument of destructive violence: the swords of Simeon and Levi are not just weapons, but the manifestation of their cruelty and thirst for vengeance (allusion to the massacres of Shechem and Hamor in Genesis 34).
3. In a broader sense, the sword symbolizes military power, judgment, or the force that is exerted. This is why the Bible will later use this image to speak of God's judgment or the power of the king.
H4380.origine: The Hebrew word מְכֵרָה (mekhérah) is related to a root that evokes the idea of splitting or cutting. Its exact etymology remains debated, but the word clearly designates a combat weapon, probably a metal sword or blade. The family of this word includes other terms related to weapons or destruction.
H4380.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 49:5, where Jacob blesses (or rather partially condemns) his sons Simeon and Levi. He uses the plural "swords" to express not only their mastery of weapons but especially their violent temperament and propensity to resort to deadly force. This passage refers to their vengeance against Shechem after the rape of their sister Dinah, an act that Jacob disapproves of. The usage is therefore very specific: it is an act of veiled reproach, a way of saying that Simeon and Levi are warriors, but that their violence is a flaw.
H4380.portee: This word reminds the reader that strength and weapons, even in the hands of believers, can be an instrument of sin if they are not submitted to God's justice and will. Jacob reproaches his sons for acting according to their anger rather than righteousness. It is a warning: possessing physical strength does not mean we have the right to use it indiscriminately. The Bible invites us to submit our power to God and His justice.

sens: father of Uzzi in the genealogy of Benjamin
H4381.detail: Micri is an ancestor of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Uzzi, who is himself the father of Ela, one of the leaders of Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:8).
H4381.origine: The name Micri comes from a Hebrew root meaning "worthy of a price" or "esteemed." It belongs to a family of names in the Old Testament that express value or merit.
H4381.emploi: Micri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:8, in the list of genealogies of Benjamin who returned to Jerusalem after the exile. He is presented as the ancestor of Ela, who is among the leaders of his tribe in the restored city.

sens: inhabitant or native of a region called Mekera
nickname or gentile applied to one of King David's elite warriors
H4382.detail:
1. Mekera designates a locality or region whose exact location is unknown, mentioned only once in the Bible. The word indicates the geographical origin of the one who is from there.
2. This gentile qualifies Hepher, one of the thirty-seven warriors listed among David's champions (1 Chronicles 11:36). These warriors constitute the king's bodyguard and are praised for their bravery and loyalty.
H4382.origine: The Hebrew word מְכֵרָתִי likely derives from a root meaning "to dig" or "to excavate," hence the possible meaning "one who digs" or "one of the digging tools." The name of the region Mekera may refer to a topographical feature: a dug place, hollowed out, or marked by the work of the earth. Like many place names in Israel, it reflects geography or a notable local activity.
H4382.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:36, in the list of the mighty warriors of King David. It qualifies Hepher, ranked among the royal military elite. No further information is given about Mekera or its inhabitants. The isolated mention of this gentile suggests that it is a minor locality in Canaan, whose memory has faded over time.

sens: Fall, act of falling or stumbling
That which causes a physical or moral fall
Obstacle that prevents progress
Hidden trap or danger
That which leads into sin
Cause of scandal or rejection
H4383.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a physical fall or stumble: when one loses balance and falls. In Leviticus 19:14, it literally refers to not placing an obstacle before a blind person that could cause them to fall.

2. It then signifies that which provokes this fall — the obstacle itself: a stone, a root, or anything that causes one to stumble. This is the sense of the trap that Ezekiel mentions in 3:20: God "will place a trap" before the righteous who turns away, meaning something that will cause them to fall.

3. Figuratively, it refers to anything that blocks or slows down an endeavor: Isaiah 57:14 speaks of removing obstacles from the people's path, in the sense of removing difficulties.

4. Morally, it is that which leads someone into evil or scandal. In Ezekiel 14:3 and 14:7, idols are "that which has caused them to fall into iniquity": they are the cause of their spiritual downfall.

5. Thus, it is also a cause of scandal or rejection — that which causes someone to be offended or refuse to believe. The word expresses the idea of encountering something that repels us.
H4383.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "kashah" (כשׁ) which means "to be hard, rigid, to obstruct." The image is that of a hard object against which one bumps. It is a noun that designates the action or the thing itself: that which causes stumbling. The word often appears in connection with the idea of guilt and responsibility: one who places a stumbling block in another's path bears moral responsibility for it.
H4383.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly among the prophets (Ezekiel notably, where it appears 9 times). Initially, in the Law (Leviticus 19:14), it concerns the concrete protection of the weak: not creating obstacles for the blind or deaf. The prophets then use it in a spiritual and moral sense: Isaiah speaks of removing material and symbolic obstacles to the people's return; Ezekiel uses it to describe what leads Israel into sin — particularly idols. The word always evokes a fall or danger, moving from the concrete (stumbling) to the spiritual (falling into sin).
H4383.portee: This word reminds the believer of two major truths: first, that our conduct affects others — we must not place obstacles in their spiritual path, but help them to advance. Secondly, that what causes us to fall does not happen by chance: it is often the things we set our eyes on (Ezekiel 14:3) that become our traps. It is an invitation to be vigilant about what we look at and covet, for therein lies the danger.

sens: that which collapses, that which lies destroyed or overturned
obstacle that causes stumbling or falling
cause of moral or spiritual downfall
H4384.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a pile of rubble, what remains of a collapsed structure. In Isaiah 3:6, at the moment of political chaos, the one who still has a garment is asked: "Take these ruins in your hand!" — that is, govern what remains of a destroyed kingdom, reduced to debris.
2. By extension, the word applies to that which causes stumbling, which blocks the way: an obstacle over which one trips. This is the meaning of the word when it speaks of idols, these "objects of scandal" (Zephaniah 1:3) that cause men to fall into idolatry and sin.
3. It can therefore designate a cause of moral or spiritual ruin: that which leads to the destruction of a person or a community, not by material collapse but by seduction to evil.
H4384.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to overturn," "to make fall." It is related to verbs expressing the idea of falling and collapsing. Its basic image is thus that of something overturned, of a mass that has collapsed — first in the literal sense (debris of stones), then in the figurative sense (moral fall, trap).
H4384.emploi: The word appears twice in the prophets. In Isaiah 3:6, at the heart of a vision of judgment on Judah, it designates the political and social debris of a collapsing kingdom: the ruin here is the final state of a city or a nation. In Zephaniah 1:3, in an announcement of universal judgment, the same word describes idols as "objects of scandal" — they are no longer just material debris, but spiritual traps, causes of destruction. The word thus pivots from the concrete (that which lies overturned) to the figurative (that which causes falling).
H4384.portee: This word reminds the reader that everything that separates from God — whether it be a fallen political system or a seductive idol — ultimately amounts to ruin and desolation. It invites one to see beyond appearances. What seems attractive or powerful may in reality be a trap that leads to destruction. It is a call to discern what builds up and what destroys.

sens: That which is traced or engraved: characters, letters, text
The text of a document or message
An official document or decree
A literary composition or song
H4385.detail:
1. It is primarily the act of writing made visible: the letters engraved on the tablets of the Law, which God Himself traced (Exodus 32:16). This designates the material mark, the inscribed form.
2. By extension, it is the content itself, the text that one reads: a writing that Hezekiah receives from the prophet Elijah (2 Chronicles 21:12), carrying a divine message.
3. It is also an authoritative document or decree: the ordinance of Cyrus, king of Persia, proclaimed verbally and confirmed "in writing" throughout his kingdom (Ezra 1:1).
4. The word even applies to a poetic composition: the song that Hezekiah composed during his healing (Isaiah 38:9).
H4385.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "ktb" (כתב), which means "to write." This root evokes the action of tracing, engraving, or marking. The word "miktav" (מִכְתָּב) thus primarily designates the instrument or result of this action: that which is written. In the Old Testament, words from this family appear wherever sacred writing, scribes, or documents are discussed.
H4385.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical and prophetic books. It first describes divine writings — the tablets of the Law written by the finger of God (Exodus 32:16 and Deuteronomy 10:4). It is then used for messages or documents carrying authority: a writing from the prophet Elijah (2 Chronicles 21:12), a royal publication displayed throughout the kingdom (Ezra 1:1). Once, it designates a sacred poetic composition: the song of Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:9). Each time, the writing carries authority and demands special attention.
H4385.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power of the written word, especially when it comes from God or His prophets. The Law of God is not a fleeting word, but inscribed, durable, engraved in stone itself — which emphasizes its solidity and definitive nature. For the Christian, it is an invitation to respect the Holy Scripture, for it is not a random oral transmission, but a fixed, authentic, and trustworthy word.

sens: Small pieces of a broken or crushed thing
Scattered fragments without useful value
Remains of a destruction
H4386.detail:
1. The word designates the small pieces resulting from the violent breaking of a fragile object. In Isaiah 30:14, the prophet describes a clay pot that is broken carelessly: the debris that results is so tiny and scattered that one cannot even use it to take fire or draw water.
2. More broadly, debris are the residual fragments of a destruction, without practical utility. The prophet's image emphasizes that the ruin will be complete and unusable: what remains can serve no purpose.
3. On a figurative level, the term evokes the idea of total and definitive loss: that which was whole has become crumbs, an image of God's judgment on pride.
H4386.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the action of striking, crushing, or pulverizing. It describes the final state of what has undergone violent destruction: not simply broken, but reduced to tiny, scattered fragments. This image of extreme fragmentation underscores the intensity of punishment or ruin.
H4386.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 30:14. The prophet uses it to intensify the judgment announced against those who refuse to listen to the word of God: their security will collapse like a clay pot reduced to debris. The uniqueness of this usage shows that it is chosen for its evocative power: debris does not designate a mere break, but a definitive pulverization, with no possibility of repair or recovery.
H4386.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment is not a mere correction: it is a radical destruction of what opposes Him. For the believer, it is a call not to place trust in fragile human structures, but in the eternal word of God.

sens: Technical term inscribed at the beginning of certain psalms to indicate their genre or mode of execution
H4387.detail: 1. The miktam is an indication present in the titles of six psalms (Psalms 16, 56, 57, 58, 59, and 60). Its exact meaning is uncertain, but it likely designates a particular type of psalm, either by its musical form, by its content, or by its liturgical use. It is unclear whether this term describes the melody to be used, the poetic structure, or the circumstances of its interpretation.
H4387.origine: The Hebrew miktam (מִכְתָּם) appears only in the titles of the psalms. Its etymology remains debated. Some scholars see a link with the word "ktm" (hidden, secret), which could suggest a psalm of intimate or confidential intercession. Others relate it to the word "engraved" or "inscribed," which would indicate a psalm composed or recorded in a particular manner. No certainty exists regarding its precise origin.
H4387.emploi: This technical term appears exclusively in the titles of the Psalms: Psalms 16, 56, 57, 58, 59, and 60 (six occurrences only). All these psalms are attributed to David. They encompass different types of prayers: psalms of trust and protection (Psalms 16, 57), psalms calling for divine vengeance (Psalms 58, 59), and psalms of lament after a military defeat (Psalms 60). This diversity of contexts makes the precise identification of the miktam difficult. The term, which does not appear anywhere else in the Bible, seems to be a specific mark of the Davidic psalter.
H4387.portee: This term emphasizes that the psalms were not merely texts to be read, but compositions to be sung or recited according to precise liturgical conventions. Although the exact meaning is lost, it reminds us that biblical worship was ordered and thoughtful, with forms adapted to different spiritual situations. For the Christian, it is an invitation to consider that even the technical and formal aspects of praise serve to honor God with order and intelligence.

sens: Hollow container made of stone or ceramic in which substances are ground and crushed with a pestle
Natural cavity in rock
Figuratively: that which reduces to nothing or completely destroys
H4388.detail:
1. The mortar is the thick bowl in which spices, herbs, or grains are crushed using a wooden or stone pestle. It is a common tool in cooking and pharmacy. Proverbs 27:22 uses it as an image of repetitive and futile work: even if one were to crush a fool in a mortar like grain, his folly would not depart — this illustrates the futility of trying to correct him.
2. The word also refers to a depression or cavity carved in rock, naturally formed. In Judges 15:19, after God split the rock, a spring gushed forth from a "cavity" called En-Hakkoré ("spring that cries"), where the exhausted Samson was able to drink and be revived.
3. Beyond the concrete object, the mortar becomes a biblical image of destruction or crushing: something or someone reduced to powder, annihilated by a superior force.
H4388.origine: The Hebrew word makh.tesh comes from a root meaning "to strike," "to break." It properly designates the object that receives the blows of the pestle and where the materials are pulverized. It is a very common instrument name in the everyday vocabulary of the ancient East.
H4388.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Proverbs 27:22 uses it in its literal and common sense: the household mortar, the utensil used for grinding. Judges 15:19 shifts it towards the concrete meaning of a rocky cavity split by God. These two uses show how the same word could refer to both the manufactured object and the natural hollow form it recalls — both receiving a "blow": one from the pestle, the other from divine trembling.
H4388.portee: For the reader, the mortar of Proverbs 27:22 is a lesson in humility: there is no correction or discipline that changes a fool if he refuses wisdom. Only God can transform the heart. In Judges 15:19, the spring gushing from the split rock manifests God's power to give life and help when all seems lost — an image of His mercy towards those who cry out to Him.

sens: Hollow region or district of Jerusalem
H4389.detail: Macthesch designates a place in the rugged terrain, probably a district or valley of Jerusalem. The Hebrew name literally means "mortar," the hollow utensil in which substances are crushed: it thus evokes a depression in the land, a low area. In Zephaniah 1:11, the prophet calls the inhabitants of this place to wail, for the merchants and the wealthy who trade there will be destroyed during divine judgment.
H4389.origine: The Hebrew word מַכְתֵּשׁ (maktesh) comes from a root meaning "to grind" or "to crush." The mortar is a deep hollow vessel, hence the figurative transition to "valley" or "hollow" of the terrain. The name of the district of Jerusalem takes up this geographical image.
H4389.emploi: Macthesch appears only once in the Bible, in Zephaniah 1:11. There it designates a specific place in Jerusalem, likely located in the city's commercial area. The prophetic context indicates that it was an active district, populated by merchants and wealthy men, destined to be struck by divine judgment on the day of the Lord.

sens: Pour a liquid or object until a container or space is completely occupied
To be full, to be filled, to contain abundantly
To completely fulfill, to bring to completion a period or a promise
To consecrate, to invest someone with a charge or function
To completely satisfy a need, desire, or request
H4390.detail:
1. To fill means to pour or put something until a container or space is maximally occupied. This is the most concrete image: one thinks of filling a cup with water, as when Genesis 24:16 speaks of filling the water jar. The idea is one of gradual accumulation until saturation.

2. To be full means to be in a state of completeness, of abundance. When Isaiah 2:8 says that "the land is filled with idols," it means that they are everywhere, in profusion. This is the resulting state of filling: no empty space. Second Kings 6:17 describes the mountain as "full" of horses and chariots of fire.

3. To accomplish means to complete what was begun or promised, to bring a process to its conclusion. When Leviticus 25:30 speaks of the "fulfillment" of a whole year, it means that the year is ending, the time has completely elapsed. This is the completion of a duration or task.

4. To consecrate or invest someone means to fill their hands with authority or responsibility by placing them in a sacred function. Exodus 28:41 and 29:9 speak of "filling" the priests, meaning to inaugurate them in their office by giving them the insignia and powers of the priesthood. The image of "filling the hand" means to entrust a mission.

5. To satisfy means to meet a need or fulfill a desire. Psalms 20:6 says that "the Lord will fulfill all your wishes," literally accomplishing them fully, satisfying them completely. It is to respond fully to an expectation.
H4390.origine: The Hebrew word מָלֵא (male) comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of fullness and filling. It is related to the concrete image of pouring or filling a container. The verb appears in several grammatical forms in Hebrew, each nuance the idea: some forms emphasize the action of filling, others the state of being full. This root is very common in Semitic languages and always retains this primary image of totality and fulfillment.
H4390.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible with 241 occurrences. It appears in very varied contexts. At the beginning of Genesis, God commands the creatures to "fill" the seas and the earth (Genesis 1:22, 1:28), expressing the idea of multiplication and occupation of space. In historical context, it describes concrete situations: the filling of vessels, of houses. In the priestly laws (Exodus 28-29, Leviticus), the verb takes on the specific meaning of "consecrating" or "investing" the priests with their function. In the Psalms and the prophets, it often takes on a spiritual dimension: fulfilling a divine promise, satisfying wishes, filling the heart with an emotion. The meaning varies according to the context, but always revolves around the idea of completeness or accomplishment.
H4390.portee: This word reminds us that God fills not only material spaces but also promises to His people. Understanding the different meanings of the word "fill" helps the reader see how the Bible speaks of divine fulfillment: what God promises, He accomplishes fully. Moreover, the idea of consecration — investing someone with a mission — shows that God entrusts important tasks to His servants. It is a word of encouragement: what God begins, He completes.

sens: Completely occupy a space, a volume
Be overwhelmed, saturated by a feeling or emotion
H4391.detail:
1. To fill a space means to occupy it entirely, to cover it completely. The stone that strikes the statue becomes a mountain and "fills the whole earth" (Daniel 2:35): it spreads everywhere, leaving nothing unoccupied.
2. To be filled with a feeling means to be completely overwhelmed, dominated by it. Nebuchadnezzar "was filled with fury" (Daniel 3:19): anger seized him entirely, took possession of him, and was visible on his face.
H4391.origine: The Aramaic root מְלָא comes from a concrete image: to make something completely occupy a place. It also exists in Hebrew in the form מָלֵא (maléa) with the same meaning. The word describes the action of leaving no void, no free space, whether it concerns a container, a territory, or the heart of a person.
H4391.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears twice in the New Testament Aramaic integrated into Daniel. In the first case (Daniel 2:35), it describes how the miraculous stone literally fills the earth — an apocalyptic image of the universal dominion of the kingdom of God. In the second case (Daniel 3:19), it describes the emotional state of the king: fury fills him, meaning it completely dominates him. These two uses show how the verb transitions from a material sense (occupying a space) to a figurative sense (being saturated with).
H4391.portee: This word reminds us that God fills the earth with His presence and reign, not by human force but by His sovereign action. It also shows that our emotions and states of mind can fill us entirely: this invites the reader to ask God to fill their heart not with anger or fear, but with His joy and peace.

sens: Containing all available space, without void
Abundant in something, possessing in large quantity
Completely filled, saturated to the maximum
Endowed, endowed with an inner quality or strength
H4392.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: a container, a field, or a place that leaves no empty space. A gold cup filled with perfume (Numbers 7:32) or a house laden with deceit (Jeremiah 5:27) are "full," entirely occupied by what they contain. This is the physical idea of saturation.
2. Abundance, wealth: a land overflowing with goods, like Israel in the time of rest, "filled" with houses and cisterns (Deuteronomy 6:11). The word denotes an overabundance, a profusion of what fills existence.
3. Moral or spiritual saturation: a cup "full" of mixed wine, a symbol of divine judgment (Psalms 75:9), or a heart "filled" with wickedness (Ecclesiastes 9:3). Fullness is not always good; it expresses a totality that can be burdensome or destructive.
4. Spiritual investiture: Joshua "filled" with the spirit of wisdom after Moses laid hands on him (Deuteronomy 34:9). The word describes a person endowed, intimately united with a divine power or quality that animates them completely.
H4392.origine: The word הִמְלֵא comes from a root meaning "to fill, to accomplish." It is an adjective that can also function as an adverb ("fully, entirely"). The family includes the verb "to fill" in the sense of the action of putting something into an empty space. The basic image is that of the transition from empty to full, from lack to totality.
H4392.emploi: This word is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (about 63 occurrences). It regularly appears in descriptions of wealth and abundance (Genesis 41:7, Deuteronomy 6:11, Nehemiah 9:25), in the rituals of the Ark and offerings (Numbers 7 passim), and in the prophets to express the saturation of divine judgment or evil. Joshua "filled with wisdom" (Deuteronomy 34:9) illustrates the spiritual use. In Jeremiah 5:27 and Ecclesiastes 9:3, fullness becomes morally ambiguous: what is full of deceit or malice. The context determines whether fullness is a blessing or condemnation.
H4392.portee: This word reminds Christians that fullness is not a matter of mechanically filling an empty space, but of saturating the soul: through divine wisdom, through justice, or through evil. The question is not "Are you filled?" but "What are you filled with?" For Joshua, being filled with wisdom meant being transformed at the very core of his being. It is an invitation to seek total integrity, not in possessions, but in character and alignment with God.

sens: What fills a container, what completely fills it
Quantity that can be held in the hand, handful
Complete set, totality of what exists or belongs to something
Multitude, large number
Entire length or extent of something
H4393.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a material fullness: what fills a container to the brim. Leviticus 16:12 speaks of "a censer full of burning coals" — it is not an empty censer, but one overflowing with glowing embers intended to carry the incense.
2. By restriction, it also designates a handful, that is, what the hand can grasp in a single take. In the same passage, the priest must take "two handfuls" of powdered incense — a practical, concrete, and precise measure.
3. Fullness also extends to the notion of totality: all that a space or a set contains. Psalms 24:1 declares that "the Lord [owns] the earth and all that it contains" — not a part, but the entirety of creation.
4. It also means an innumerable multitude. Genesis 48:19 announces that Ephraim's younger brother "will become a multitude of nations" — a descendant so numerous that it fills several peoples.
5. There is also the idea of full length or complete extent. Isaiah 8:8 speaks of one who will fill the earth "in all its extent," covering the entire territory.
H4393.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root מלא ("to fill"): it literally designates what fills another. Its variants include verbal forms and the adjective "full." The basic image is very concrete: a filled container, a hand filled with something, a space occupied in its entirety. It is a very common word in everyday Hebrew language.
H4393.emploi: This word appears 36 times in the Old Testament. It is used in practical and ritual contexts (the measures of worship), as in Leviticus 16:12 or Exodus 16:32 where it concerns braziers and filled containers. It also describes the totality of what exists: "the earth and all that it contains" (Psalms 24:1), or the beings that inhabit a space (Isaiah 42:10: "you who sail on the sea and you who populate it"). Genesis 48:19 applies it to future descendants, a "multitude." It also designates full stature or length: in 1 Samuel 28:20, Saul falls "from all his height." The word thus encompasses the idea of completeness, of totality filled, from the smallest measure (handful) to the largest (the entire creation).
H4393.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God possesses the fullness of all things: the whole earth and everything it contains belongs to Him (Psalms 24:1). It invites us to recognize that what seems great to us — a multitude of nations, an endless expanse — is always under the gaze and authority of the God who fills all. It is also a word that speaks to the soul: what can fill our hands, satisfy our days, fulfill our aspirations is only fully satisfying when we acknowledge the fullness that comes from God.

sens: Action of placing, embedding precious stones in an object
Solemn installation of a person into a sacred function
Ritualized ceremony that confers an official religious role to someone
H4394.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the work of the goldsmith: embedding precious stones so that they remain securely in place. Exodus 25:7 speaks of "onyx stones and other stones for the setting of the ephod and the breastplate" — gems embedded in the garments of the high priest.
2. By extension, "consecration" describes the official installation of priests: a ritual ceremony where God establishes them in their sacred function. Exodus 29:26 recounts the sacrifice of the ram "at the consecration of Aaron" — the animal that Moses burns to inaugurate Aaron as high priest.
3. The underlying idea is that one "places" someone, one "fixes" them in a role, just as one fixes a stone in a piece of jewelry. Leviticus 8:28 states that this consecration sacrifice ascends to the Lord, marking the beginning of the priest's sacred function.
H4394.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to fill," "to complete." The same imagery is found in the expression "to fill the hand" — a Hebrew idiomatic phrase that specifically refers to consecration to the priesthood. The word implies a transition: before consecration, one is incomplete for the role; afterward, one is "filled" with this charge and bears all the responsibility before God.
H4394.emploi: The word appears about fifteen times, almost entirely in the books of Exodus and Leviticus, which describe the organization of worship and the Israelite priesthood. It denotes two realities: first, the work of goldsmiths (Exodus 25:7 and 35:9, where it refers to setting stones); secondly, and primarily, the eight days of ceremony where Moses consecrates Aaron and his sons (Exodus 29 and Leviticus 8). Leviticus 7:37 lists the various sacrifices of the Law, including "the consecration." The word appears only once outside the Pentateuch (1 Chronicles 29:2), where it regains the meaning of "setting" or "decoration."
H4394.portee: For the Christian, this word evokes two truths. First, the idea that God "fixes" His servants in a specific role, not out of whim but through a solemn and irrevocable act. Secondly, the image of the embedded stone reminds us that our personal consecration — our commitment to serve God — places us within a framework: we are not free to do as we please, but "set" within the divine will, which gives us stability and meaning.

sens: What grows and is harvested from the land
The first harvest offered to God
The fruit of agricultural labor
H4395.detail:
1. The word literally refers to what grows and is harvested from the land: the fruits of the harvest, the grapes of the vintage, everything that the soil produces. In Exodus 22:29, it speaks of the "firstfruits" of the harvest and the vintage, meaning the first portions of these crops.
2. By extension, it specifically denotes the first harvest that Israel offered to God in gratitude for His blessing. The word evokes the idea of fullness and fertility: the land gives its full produce. In Numbers 18:27, the "new wine" (fresh grape juice) is counted as an offering on par with the grain from the threshing floor.
3. Generally, it signifies the concrete result of agricultural work: it is what one obtains when cultivating the land. In Deuteronomy 22:9, the text speaks of the "produce" of the vine and what has been sown in it, showing that mixing seeds causes both the expected harvest and that of the vine to be lost.
H4395.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of filling and abundance: something full and overflowing. This is the sense of "fullness" or "that which fills." In Hebrew, the same root is used to express the notion of fulfillment and satisfaction. The word thus evokes the image of a generous harvest, a crop that fills the granaries.
H4395.emploi: The word appears three times in the Torah. It always denotes a specific agricultural product: the firstfruits (Exodus 22:29), the new wine of the vintage (Numbers 18:27), and the produce of the crops (Deuteronomy 22:9). These three uses show that the term applies to what comes from the fields and vineyards. It is a word from Israel's agricultural and ritual law, linked to the commandments concerning offerings and the proper use of the land.
H4395.portee: This word reminds the Christian that all fruit of their labor comes from God and should be offered to Him first. It teaches gratitude towards the Creator and the importance of not confusing goods, respecting the order that God establishes. Recognizing that the land produces "by the grace of God" directs the heart towards worship.
