sens: Mounting, frame, or mount designed to hold a precious stone in place
Metallic setting that surrounds and secures a stone
Action of embedding, mounting a stone in a metal
H4396.detail: 1. A setting is the frame or mount that holds a precious stone in place. In the context of the high priest's breastplate, each stone was placed in a gold setting that encased and protected it: "These stones shall be set in their gold settings" (Exodus 28:20). The imagery is that of a stone surrounded and secured by metal, like a diamond in a ring. 2. By extension, a setting also refers to the overall mounting or frame where the stones are inserted. On the high priest's breastplate, there were several rows of precious stones, each in its own setting: "You shall set in it a setting of stones, four rows of stones" (Exodus 28:17). 3. The word can also refer to the very action of placing a stone in its mount: to set means to place a stone in its metal frame.
H4396.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to fill" or "to complete." The setting "completes" the stone by providing it with its protective frame: it makes it complete and functional. It is the name corresponding to the verb that describes the action of mounting a stone.
H4396.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the description of the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28 and 39). It is a technical and concrete term: the gold setting was the essential mounting that held the twelve precious stones of the breastplate. The first two uses (Exodus 28:17 and 28:20) describe the instructions given for making the breastplate; the third (Exodus 39:13) recounts its completion. The term is used strictly in a concrete sense, without figurative nuance.
H4396.portee: This word reminds us that the most beautiful stones need a setting to be valued and protected. Similarly, the high priest's breastplate, adorned with embedded stones, symbolizes the beauty and solidity of the priestly ministry before God. It is an invitation to recognize that beauty often comes from a good structure, a good frame.

sens: Person sent to convey a message or mission
Official representative of a sovereign or authority
Servant or agent assigned a task
Celestial being in the service of God
H4397G.detail:
1. The messenger is primarily one who is sent to deliver a word: Jacob sends messengers to Esau (Genesis 32:3), Israel sends messengers to neighboring kings to request passage (Judges 11:17). They serve as intermediaries of communication between two parties.
2. A messenger can also be the official emissary of a king or power: Hezekiah receives messengers from the king of Assyria (2 Kings 19:23), who speak on behalf of the sovereign with his authority. The messenger embodies the one who sends them.
3. The messenger also carries out practical tasks: they seek, summon, and convey orders. David sends messengers to gather provisions or recruit soldiers (1 Samuel 11:7), and Abigail follows David's messengers (1 Samuel 25:42).
4. In theology, this word refers to angels — beings sent by God. The Psalms speak of God who "makes his angels messengers" (Psalms 104:4), superhuman creatures in divine service.
H4397G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to send" or "to delegate": the messenger is literally "one who is sent." The same root gives rise to words for sending or mission. In biblical Greek, this Hebrew word is often translated as "aggelos" (aggelos), which means exactly "sent one" and refers to both a human messenger and a celestial angel — the notion of "sent one" applies to both.
H4397G.emploi: The word appears 96 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical narratives (Genesis, Judges, Samuel, Kings). Its primary usage is almost always concrete: kings, leaders, and owners send messengers to negotiate, request, order, or seek someone. It is the everyday vocabulary of diplomacy and administration. Over time, the meaning elevates: prophets are sometimes called "messengers" of God (2 Chronicles 36:15), and finally, celestial beings in the service of God bear this name. In all cases, the idea remains the same: a sent one who represents the one who sends and conveys their will.
H4397G.portee: This word shows us that God communicates with humans through intermediaries — messengers who carry His word. Whether human (prophets, servants) or celestial (angels), they embody God's concern to remain in relationship with His people. Understanding that angels are "sent ones" helps to grasp that they are never autonomous: they always act to fulfill God's mission.

sens: Sent one, messenger assigned a mission
Spiritual creature serving God
The angel of the Lord, manifested divine presence
Celestial being worshiped and praised before the throne of God
H4397H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a messenger, someone sent to convey a message or accomplish a mission. Thus, in Judges 2:1, "an angel of the Lord" comes up from Gilgal to remind the Israelites of God's covenant: it is a bearer of divine word.
2. It refers to a spiritual being created by God, distinct from humanity, who serves and glorifies Him. Psalm 103:20 describes them as creatures who execute His word and listen to His voice.
3. The expression "the angel of the Lord" refers to a special manifestation of divine presence and action in the world. In Genesis 16:7-11, this angel speaks to Hagar and promises her descendants in the name of the Lord; in 1 Chronicles 21:16, David sees him holding the sword that threatens Jerusalem — it is God acting through this angel.
4. In heaven, angels form a celestial court that worships and serves God (Psalms 148:2). They are powerful spirits: one angel destroys one hundred eighty-five thousand Assyrians in a single night (Isaiah 37:36).
H4397H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to send." An angel is therefore fundamentally one who is sent, a messenger. In biblical Hebrew, the same word can refer to a simple human courier — but in most cases, it refers to spiritual beings sent by God. The Hebrew Bible uses this term 101 times, primarily for celestial creatures in the service of the Lord.
H4397H.emploi: The word appears 101 times in the Old Testament, first in Genesis with celestial appearances to Abraham, Hagar, and Jacob. It is mostly found in deliverance narratives (the angel who guides the Israelites in the desert, Exodus 14:19) and in critical moments when God intervenes (the angel who stops Balaam, Numbers 22; the angel who turns aside David's sword, 2 Samuel 24:16). The Psalms celebrate angels as servants of God (Psalms 103:20; 148:2). An important nuance: "the angel of the Lord" in particular seems to be a form of theophany, that is, a direct manifestation of God, as this angel speaks in the name of the Lord and acts with His absolute authority.
H4397H.portee: Believing in angels means recognizing that God does not abandon His people: He keeps, guides, and protects them through His messengers. Angels remind us that the visible world is not all; there exists a spiritual reality where God reigns with His celestial court. For the Christian, this angelic presence is a source of confidence: God has placed His creatures in service to those who inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14).

sens: messenger sent by God
celestial creature in the service of God
divine protector
H4398.detail:
1. An angel is primarily a messenger, someone whom God sends to accomplish a mission. The word comes from the verb "to send": the angel is the one who will deliver God's message. In Daniel 3:28, Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges that the God of Israel has "sent His angel" to save Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the fiery furnace — it is a powerful creature that God dispatches to intervene.
2. An angel is a celestial creature, a superhuman being who belongs to the court of God and obeys His commands. He is not a man, but a servant in the invisible world.
3. An angel is a protector: he acts to defend those whom God loves. In Daniel 6:22, the angel shuts the mouths of the lions to protect Daniel, because the king of heaven judges him innocent. This is a sign of divine benevolence toward His servants.
H4398.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to send, dispatch." The angel is therefore, by his very name, one who is sent — a messenger. The related Hebrew term (mal'akh) is found throughout the Bible with the same meaning. He is not an imaginary creature, but in biblical thought, a real being that exists in the invisible world, in the service of the living God.
H4398.emploi: The word appears twice in the book of Daniel, an Aramaic text. In both cases, it is God who sends His angel for a miraculous action: to deliver from fire and to shut the mouths of lions. These appearances of angels mark God's direct intervention on behalf of His faithful servants. Daniel and his companions recognize divine protection through the action of the angel.
H4398.portee: These two accounts encourage the believer: when one remains faithful to God even at the cost of their life, God Himself intervenes through His angels to protect us. The angel reminds us that we are never alone in the face of opposition or danger — there is an invisible reality of divine power watching over us.

sens: Action of doing, accomplishing something; result of that action
Manual or artisanal labor; what is made or constructed
Religious service or function in worship
Activity, occupation, or profession
Business, enterprise, or project
Property, possession, or belongings
H4399.detail:
1. The primary meaning refers to the accomplishment of an action: what is done, realized. God "completed His work on the seventh day" (Genesis 2:2) — what He created. It is the concrete result of an activity, large or small.

2. Very often, the word describes the work of artisans and laborers: the making of the tent of meeting, metalwork, carpentry. In Exodus 36:5, the people bring much more "than is needed to carry out the work" of the sanctuary. It refers to technical labor, craftsmanship.

3. In a religious context, "work" refers to the functions of worship, the service in the sanctuary. The priests "performed all the duties in the Most Holy Place" (1 Chronicles 6:49) — what must be accomplished as service to God.

4. The word can simply refer to daily work, regular occupation. It is what one does "six days" according to the commandment (Exodus 20:9).

5. It is also used for a business, an enterprise that one conducts. Thus a great "work" that is accomplished together (Nehemiah 6:16).

6. Finally, "work" can refer to property, what belongs to you and has been acquired through labor.
H4399.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to do, to accomplish." It is from the same family as verbs related to action and realization. The starting image is that of action leading to a result, doing that produces a concrete outcome. It is a fundamental word in the Old Testament for speaking of any intentional activity, from divine creative work to human labor.
H4399.emploi: The word appears 149 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Pentateuch (the first five books), Chronicles, and historical books. It is very frequent in Exodus, where it describes the works of the tabernacle and its furnishings. It is also found in the Sabbath prescriptions, to denote the "servile work" prohibited on the seventh day (Numbers 28:25). Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context: creative work with God (Genesis 2:2), artisanal work for worship (Exodus 36), liturgical service with Aaron (1 Chronicles 6:49), or ordinary secular activity (Exodus 20:9). It is a neutral term that encompasses all types of human or divine activity.
H4399.portee: This word reminds us that all work, from the humblest to the greatest, has value in the eyes of God. The "work" of God in creation invites the believer to see their own work as participating in the good order that God has established. The Sabbath rest, where one refrains from "servile work," teaches that both rest and work are necessary for a just life. Finally, accomplishing a "work" for God, such as worship or service, is responding to His call.

sens: State of what exists or occurs in large quantities
Generosity, profusion in giving or distribution
H4342.detail:
1. The word evokes abundance, that which overflows, that which exists in very large quantities. In Job 36:31, God provides food in abundance: this means that He generously and without stinginess meets the needs of His people.
2. By extension, it also refers to generosity in action, the profusion of giving. When God gives abundantly, He does not give drop by drop, but in an overflowing and gratifying manner.
H4342.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be numerous, to increase" (in its intensive form called Hiphil). This form indicates an active process, a voluntary multiplication. The root expresses the idea of growth and amplification, from which the meaning of abundance as multiplication and profusion naturally derives.
H4342.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. It is used in Job 36:31 in the context of a meditation on divine providence: Elihu explains how God governs the peoples and how He nourishes humanity abundantly. It is in a speech of praise for God's works and goodness, emphasizing His ability to provide without limitation.
H4342.portee: This term reminds Christians that God is not stingy in His gifts. It invites us to see divine generosity as a characteristic of His nature: God abundantly provides for our true needs. It is a call to trust in His Providence rather than to live in fear of lack.

sens: Character from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the genealogy of Caleb
H4343.detail: Macbena is a man from the tribe of Judah who appears only in the genealogical list of 1 Chronicles 2:49. He is the son of Sheva and the grandson of Caleb, placing him in the lineage of great figures of the people of Israel. We know of him only his place in this family genealogy.
H4343.origine: The name Macbena literally means "link" or "chain." It marks this man's belonging to the tribe of Judah and to the powerful lineage of Caleb, one of Israel's most famous ancestors. The name reflects the importance of family ties in the culture of God's people.
H4343.emploi: Macbena is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:49, in the heart of a genealogy that lists the descendants of Caleb. This passage exposes the family ties in the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy period and shows how the tribe preserved the memory of its great families. His unique mention confirms that he was a minor figure, important only for his role in the continuity of the lineage.

sens: Gadite warrior in the service of King David
H4344.detail: Macbannai is a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David at Ziklag. He appears in the list of military leaders who rallied to David and was ranked eleventh in the enumeration of these valiant men (1 Chronicles 12:13).
H4344.origine: The name Macbannai means "link of the Lord" or "chain of the Lord" in Hebrew, formed from two elements: makh (link, chain) and Bannaï (of the Lord). This name evokes a bond, a union under divine protection.
H4344.emploi: Macbannai appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:13. He is mentioned among the warriors of Gad who crossed the Jordan to support David when he was pursued by Saul. His inclusion in this official list shows that he was a man of military and social importance, worthy of being listed alongside the other valiant fighters of the king.

sens: Assembly of bars or crossed rods forming a lattice
Openwork structure used to hold or sift
Base of an altar allowing the passage of ashes and liquids
H4345.detail:
1. The grate is a structure made of crossed bars or rods, like a lattice. In Exodus 27:4, Moses is instructed to make a "grate of bronze, in the form of a lattice" for the altar of burnt offerings: it is not a solid surface, but an openwork structure that allows light and fluids to pass through.
2. Concretely, this grate serves to hold the wood and the sacrificial animals while allowing the ashes and blood to drain down. It thus plays the role of a sieve or strainer, separating what remains from what falls.
3. Placed "below the rim of the altar, from the bottom to halfway up" (Exodus 38:4), the grate is embedded in the very structure of the altar, held by four rings (Exodus 38:5). It is not a detachable accessory, but an integral part of the worship.
H4345.origine: The Hebrew word מִכְבָּר (mikhbár) comes from the root כָּבַר (kavar), which originally means "to weave" or "to intertwine." The grate thus evokes the image of a woven fabric, hence its meaning of "lattice" or "openwork structure." This image of interlacing explains why it applies to a structure where bars cross each other.
H4345.emploi: The word appears six times in Exodus, always in relation to the altar of burnt offerings. It specifically designates the bronze lattice that forms the base and internal structure of this altar. The six occurrences are spread across construction instructions (Exodus 27:4), the enumeration of materials (Exodus 35:16; Exodus 39:39), and the actual account of the altar's construction (Exodus 38:4, 38:5, 38:30). In each context, the grate is always mentioned with its rings, bars, and related utensils, forming a functional whole.
H4345.portee: The grate of the altar reminds us that sacrifice requires a precise structure, established by God Himself. Its openwork character symbolizes the transparency of worship: nothing is hidden, everything passes through. For the believer, it is an invitation to offer one's worship openly, fully aware that God sees everything, inside and out.
